title: The abelian category of sheaves
notes: Kernels are defined sectionwise and cokernels by associating a sheaf to the sectionwise cokernel; Exercise 2 identifies kernel of the cokernel with cokernel of the kernel.
statement: For a topological space \(X\), sheaves of complex vector spaces form an abelian category. For \(f:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G\), \((\ker f)(U)=\ker(\mathcal F(U)\to\mathcal G(U))\), while \(\operatorname{coker}f\) is the sheafification of the sectionwise cokernel; \(\operatorname{coim}f\simeq\operatorname{im}f\).
fate: This is pre-seminar sheaf homological algebra; see \citet[\S 3]{grothendieck1957homological} and the modern sheafification construction in \citet[Tag 007X]{stacks2026foundations}.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, this remains the standard abelian-category structure; the sectionwise cokernel need not itself be a sheaf.

title: Sheafification and its universal property
notes: The notes glue compatible local representatives, denote the associated sheaf by \(C^+\), and require unique factorization of every map from \(C\) to a sheaf.
statement: For every presheaf \(C\) of complex vector spaces there is a sheaf \(aC\) and a map \(C\to aC\) such that \(\operatorname{Hom}(aC,\mathcal F)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(C,\mathcal F)\) naturally for every sheaf \(\mathcal F\); \(C_x\to(aC)_x\) is an isomorphism for every \(x\).
reconstruction: The stalk formulation disambiguates the abbreviated gluing description; a single compatible-family plus construction requires a separated input, or a second application.
fate: \citet[Lemmas 6.17.1--6.17.2 and the following universal property, Tag 007X]{stacks2026foundations} gives the construction. The notation \(C^+\) here names the completed associated sheaf, not necessarily one application of the usual plus construction.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the universal property uniquely determines sheafification up to unique isomorphism.

title: Exactness is tested on stalks
notes: Exercise 3 says a sequence of sheaves is exact if and only if all its stalk sequences are exact.
statement: A sequence \(\mathcal F_1\to\mathcal F_2\to\mathcal F_3\) of sheaves of vector spaces on \(X\) is exact at \(\mathcal F_2\) if and only if \((\mathcal F_1)_x\to(\mathcal F_2)_x\to(\mathcal F_3)_x\) is exact for every \(x\in X\).
fate: Sheafification preserves stalks, and filtered colimits of vector spaces are exact; this is part of the classical sheaf formalism of \citet[\S 3]{grothendieck1957homological}.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the statement holds without separation or local-compactness assumptions on the space.

title: Flabby sheaves and the local-system caveat
notes: A sheaf is called flabby when every section on an open subset extends to all of \(X\). The following sentence says that locally constant sheaves are not flabby.
statement: \(\mathcal F\) is flabby if \(\mathcal F(X)\to\mathcal F(U)\) is surjective for every open \(U\subset X\), equivalently all open restriction maps are surjective. A nonzero constant sheaf on a connected locally connected space with a disconnected open subset is not flabby. The zero sheaf and every sheaf on a discrete space give exceptions to a blanket claim about local systems.
reconstruction: The extra topological and nonzero hypotheses state the situation illustrated by the notebook drawing.
fate: The definition and acyclicity are classical; \citet[Definition 20.12.1 and Lemma 20.12.3, Tag 09SV]{stacks2026foundations}. The exceptions follow directly from the definition.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the definition is correct, but the unqualified assertion about locally constant sheaves is false.

title: Sheaves and flabby sheaves on a finite poset
notes: Problem 4 equips a finite poset \(P\) with \(\overline{\{x\}}=\{y:y\le x\}\), asks for sheaves as representations, and asks which are flabby.
statement: With upper sets open, a sheaf on finite \(P\) is equivalently a covariant functor \(F:P\to\operatorname{Vect}_{\mathbb C}\). Its sections on an upper set \(U\) are \(\varprojlim_{x\in U}F(x)\). It is flabby exactly when \(F(x)\to\varprojlim_{y>x}F(y)\) is surjective for every \(x\in P\), with the empty limit zero.
reconstruction: The inverse-limit criterion and its two-direction argument are our explicit solution of the recorded exercise. \ours{} The stated short argument is supplied in this companion.
fate: The diagram description is elementary sheaf theory; the stated flabbiness test is reconstructed directly: extend a compatible section over an upper set by adding its remaining points in reverse order. Necessity follows by restricting from \(\{y:y\ge x\}\) to \(\{y:y>x\}\). Compare the definition in \citet[Tag 09SV]{stacks2026foundations}.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the exercise has this finite and effective answer; surjectivity on individual comparable pairs alone is insufficient at branching points.

title: Combinatorial sheaves and the poset of strata
notes: The map sending a point to its stratum is said to induce an equivalence from sheaves on the poset of strata to combinatorial sheaves on \(X\).
statement: For a finite regular cell complex with its face poset, cellular sheaves can be encoded by vector spaces on cells and compatible maps along face inclusions. For an arbitrary stratification the stated equivalence requires additional hypotheses: its exact truth depends on what is meant here by a combinatorial sheaf and on incidence and monodromy data.
reconstruction: The regular-cell formulation is a limited modern interpretation, not a claim that the notebook imposed that condition.
fate: The finite-poset assertion is precise, but the notes refer back to definitions in a previous notebook. The present pages do not provide the assumptions needed to identify the claimed equivalence for all stratifications; the general sheaf formalism in \citet[\S 3]{grothendieck1957homological} does not supply them automatically.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, a standard cellular interpretation is available, while the unrestricted stratified-space claim cannot be certified from this record alone.

title: Exactness of sections when the kernel is flabby
notes: The left-exact global-section functor becomes exact on a short exact sequence when its first term is flabby.
statement: If \(0\to\mathcal F\to\mathcal G\to\mathcal H\to0\) is exact and \(\mathcal F\) is flabby, then \(0\to\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)\to\Gamma(X,\mathcal G)\to\Gamma(X,\mathcal H)\to0\) is exact.
fate: \citet[Lemma 20.12.3 and its proof, Tag 09SV]{stacks2026foundations} proves precisely the needed lifting property. It belongs to the older flabby-resolution method.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the assertion is valid on every topological space.

title: Flabby resolutions and sheaf cohomology
notes: Every sheaf embeds in a flabby one; iterating on cokernels gives a resolution, and its global-section cohomology is independent of the resolution.
statement: For every sheaf \(\mathcal F\), the map into the sheaf \(U\mapsto\prod_{x\in U}\mathcal F_x\) is injective and the target is flabby. Iteration gives \(0\to\mathcal F\to I^0\to I^1\to\cdots\). The groups \(H^i(\Gamma(X,I^\bullet))\) are independent of a chosen flabby resolution and equal \(R^i\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)\).
reconstruction: The product-of-stalks construction makes the asserted embedding explicit; independence is via the acyclic-resolution comparison theorem.
fate: \citet[\S 3]{grothendieck1957homological} supplies the derived-functor framework; flabby acyclicity is checked in \citet[Lemma 20.12.3, Tag 09SV]{stacks2026foundations}. This is exposition, not a new 1987 construction.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the resolution computes sheaf cohomology in all nonnegative degrees.

title: Cohomology with compact supports
notes: The same resolution construction is proposed with compactly supported sections on a locally compact space.
statement: For a locally compact Hausdorff space \(X\), \(\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)\) consists of sections with compact support, and \(H_c^i(X,\mathcal F)=R^i\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)\). A resolution by \(c\)-soft sheaves, in particular an appropriate flabby resolution, computes these groups.
reconstruction: Hausdorffness and the acyclicity condition are supplied explicitly.
fate: This is the standard compact-support construction underlying the duality formalism already presented in \citet[Chapters II--III]{hartshorne1966residues}; only the publisher chapter metadata was reopened for that older volume.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the locally compact Hausdorff setting gives the usual compact-support theory; unrestricted support claims require a specified family of supports.

title: The dual of compactly supported sections
notes: The last construction sets \(\mathcal F^*(V)=\Gamma_c(V,\mathcal F)^*\), with restrictions dual to extension by zero, and relates it to flabbiness.
statement: For sheaves of complex vector spaces on locally compact Hausdorff \(X\), set \(D_c\mathcal F(U)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(\Gamma_c(U,\mathcal F),\mathbb C)\). If \(\mathcal F\) is \(c\)-soft, compact-support Mayer--Vietoris makes this presheaf a sheaf. Its restriction maps are surjective because linear functionals extend from vector subspaces, so it is flabby.
reconstruction: The sufficient c-soft hypothesis and the Mayer--Vietoris explanation specify the missing sheaf condition.
fate: This is the elementary compact-support dual used in derived duality; compare the 1966 duality framework \citep[Chapters II--III]{hartshorne1966residues}. It is not an assertion that naive pointwise dualization of an arbitrary sheaf is Verdier duality.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the construction is valid under the stated acyclicity condition; derived duality requires applying it to a suitable complex.

title: Dyson's constant-term identity
notes: For nonnegative integral \(a_j\), the constant term of \(F(x;a)=\prod_{i\ne j}(1-x_j/x_i)^{a_j}\) is asserted to be \((\sum a_j)!/\prod a_j!\).
statement: For every \(n\ge1\) and \(a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^n\), \[\operatorname{CT}_{x_1,\ldots,x_n}\prod_{i\ne j}(1-x_j/x_i)^{a_j}=\frac{(a_1+\cdots+a_n)!}{a_1!\cdots a_n!}.\]
fate: \citet[p.~1884]{good1970short} states this exact identity and records the 1962 proofs by Gunson and Wilson; Good's paper was received 26 December 1969 and published June 1970.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the identity is an established theorem, and the seminar occurrence is expository.

title: Good's interpolation recurrence
notes: Interpolation is applied to a function printed as identically zero, but the ensuing sum is one and is used to reduce the exponents one at a time.
statement: For distinct nonzero \(x_i\), interpolation of \(1\) gives \(\sum_j\prod_{i\ne j}(1-x_j/x_i)^{-1}=1\). Thus the constant terms satisfy \(G(a)=\sum_jG(a-e_j)\) if all \(a_j>0\), the deletion rule when \(a_j=0\), and \(G(0)=1\). These rules uniquely determine the multinomial coefficient.
fate: The complete proof is \citet[p.~1884, equations (1)--(3)]{good1970short}. The source explicitly interpolates the constant function one.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the proof works after correcting that constant; no limiting interpretation of a zero exponent is needed.

title: Geodesics and the constrained Neumann equation
notes: The two columns write \(\ddot q=\lambda Aq\) on \((Aq,q)=1\), and \(x^{\prime\prime}=-Ax+ux\) on \(|x|^2=1\).
statement: Let \(A\) be positive definite symmetric. A geodesic \(q(s)\) on \(q^TAq=1\), in arclength, satisfies \(q_{ss}=\lambda Aq\), where \(\lambda=-q_s^TAq_s/\|Aq\|^2\). Motion on the unit sphere in potential \(x^TAx/2\) satisfies \(x^{\prime\prime}=-Ax+ux\), with \(u=x^TAx-\|x^{\prime}\|^2\).
reconstruction: Positive definiteness and arclength fix the ellipsoid case and the signs of the multipliers.
fate: These constrained equations are classical. The derivation and normalization are reproduced by \citet[\S\S 2--4]{veselovwu2020geodesic}, whose later work explicitly distinguishes Kn\"orrer's 1982 theorem from its own hyperboloid scattering results.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, both equations follow directly by differentiating their constraints.

title: Knörrer's Gauss-map correspondence
notes: The notes credit H. Kn\"orrer, 1982: after changing the parameter, \(x=Aq/|Aq|\) takes geodesics into Neumann trajectories.
statement: For a nonconstant ellipsoid geodesic as above, choose \(d\tau/ds=\sqrt{-\lambda(s)}\). Then \(x(\tau)=Aq(\tau)/\|Aq(\tau)\|\) satisfies the Neumann equation with matrix \(A\). The image is a fixed level of an additional Neumann integral; it is not all Neumann trajectories for the one fixed quadric.
reconstruction: The explicit time change and restriction on the converse are supplied from the primary later calculation.
fate: \citet[Theorem 4.1, equations (28)--(33)]{veselovwu2020geodesic} gives the calculation and explicitly attributes it to Knörrer 1982. The original DOI was located \citep{knorrer1982geodesics}, but the original full paper could not be opened.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the forward correspondence is established; the extra integral matters for a converse.

title: The scalar spectral operator and its gauge transform
notes: Each coordinate is an eigenfunction of \(L=-d^2/dt^2+u\); a first-derivative operator \(\widetilde L=-d^2/dt^2+v\,d/dt\) is called conjugate to it by the Gauss or Miura substitution.
statement: If \(x_i^{\prime\prime}=-a_ix_i+ux_i\), then \(Lx_i=a_ix_i\). For \(r>0\) with \(v=2r^{\prime}/r\), \[r^{-1}(-D^2+vD)r=-D^2+\frac{v^2}{4}-\frac{v^{\prime}}2.\] In the Gauss substitution take \(r=\|Aq\|\), so constant multiplication by \(A\) commutes with these scalar operators.
reconstruction: The gauge multiplier, potential, interval, and absence of an imposed operator domain are made explicit. \oursComputed{} The independent checks are recorded in the early-record verification log.
fate: The first identity is immediate from the differential equation. The gauge calculation is independently expanded here; it agrees with the time-change calculation in \citet[\S 4]{veselovwu2020geodesic}.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, this is an operator conjugacy on any interval where the multiplier is nonzero, not a global spectral assertion without boundary conditions.

title: Recovering a rank-one perturbation from its spectrum
notes: Gelfand fixes a symmetric matrix \(A\), gives the eigenvalues of \(A+K\) with \(\operatorname{rank}K=1\), and asks how to recover \(K\).
statement: For \(A=\operatorname{diag}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n)\) with distinct real entries and symmetric positive rank-one \(K=vv^T\), a prescribed characteristic polynomial \(p_\beta(z)=\prod_j(z-\beta_j)\) requires \[v_i^2=-\frac{p_\beta(\alpha_i)}{\prod_{k\ne i}(\alpha_i-\alpha_k)}.\] Nonnegative right sides, with at least one strictly positive, are necessary and sufficient for rank exactly one. The signs of nonzero \(v_i\), modulo a common sign, remain undetermined. For arbitrary \(K=uv^T\), only the products \(u_iv_i\) are recovered.
reconstruction: Simple spectrum, positivity, and the distinction between a matrix and its diagonal-sign-conjugacy class are additional assumptions; the residue argument is our verification. \oursComputed{} The independent checks are recorded in the early-record verification log.
fate: The matrix determinant lemma yields \(p_\beta(z)/p_\alpha(z)=1-\sum_i v_i^2/(z-\alpha_i)\); taking residues proves the formula. This is a classical rank-one secular equation, related to the spectral viewpoint in \citet[\S 2]{veselovwu2020geodesic}, but the notebook's bare reconstruction question is not uniquely solvable.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the normalized symmetric inverse problem is explicit; uniqueness of the matrix in a fixed basis is false without extra data.
speaker: I. M. Gelfand

title: The Euclidean Lie--Poisson realization of Neumann motion
notes: The notes set \(M=[\dot x,x]\), \(p=x\), use the standard \(e(3)\) brackets, and take \(H=(M^2+(Ap,p))/2\).
statement: With \(\varepsilon_{123}=1\), brackets \(\{M_i,M_j\}=\varepsilon_{ijk}M_k\), \(\{M_i,p_j\}=\varepsilon_{ijk}p_k\), \(\{p_i,p_j\}=0\), and convention \(\dot f=\{f,H\}\), the Hamiltonian gives \(\dot p=M\times p\) and \(\dot M=(Ap)\times p\). On \(p^2=1\), \(M\cdot p=0\), one has \(M=p\times\dot p\) and \(\ddot p=-Ap+(p^TAp-\dot p^2)p\).
reconstruction: Orientation and Hamiltonian-vector-field conventions are specified to make the sign comparison meaningful. \oursComputed{} The independent checks are recorded in the early-record verification log.
fate: The equations are verified by contracting the displayed brackets; the Neumann normalization agrees with \citet[\S 3]{veselovwu2020geodesic}. The handwritten \([\dot x,x]\) has the opposite sign under the usual cross-product convention.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the Hamiltonian realization is standard, with the momentum sign corrected or an opposite cross-product convention declared.

title: The second bracket fails Jacobi as written
notes: The second table reads \(\{M_i,M_j\}_2=\varepsilon_{ijk}a_kM_k\), \(\{M_i,p_j\}_2=\varepsilon_{ijk}a_kp_k\), \(\{p_i,p_j\}_2=\varepsilon_{ijk}M_k\), with \(F=p^2/2\). It is said to give another Hamiltonian description.
statement: The displayed table is not a Poisson bracket for a general diagonal \(A\): its Jacobiator on \((M_1,p_1,p_2)\) is \((a_3-a_2)M_2\). Its formal vector field for \(F=p^2/2\) is also the negative of the first recorded flow. One algebraically valid repair keeps \(\{M_i,M_j\}_2=\varepsilon_{ijk}a_kM_k\), changes \(\{M_i,p_j\}_2\) to \(\varepsilon_{ijk}a_jp_k\), and changes \(\{p_i,p_j\}_2\) to \(-\varepsilon_{ijk}M_k\). This repaired bracket is Poisson and gives \(\dot M=Ap\times p,\ \dot p=M\times p\) with the same \(F\).
reconstruction: The mixed coefficient and the momentum-momentum sign are changed explicitly; simply reversing time does not cure the failed Jacobi identity. \oursComputed{} The independent checks are recorded in the early-record verification log.
fate: The scan confirms the literal indices and sign. The Jacobi counterexample, all coordinate Jacobi identities for the repaired table, and the two Hamiltonian vector fields are independently calculated in the accompanying script. The underlying Neumann system is classical \citep[\S 3]{veselovwu2020geodesic}; that citation is not an exact source for this chosen repair. The independent associative-matrix construction in Section~\ref{dev:poisson-repair} proves Jacobi and compatibility for the repair.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the literal second Hamiltonian description is false; the displayed repair is a verified reconstruction, not a uniquely established reading of the intended historical formula.

title: Combinatorial sheaves as representations, recalled
notes: The opening reminder assigns objects to points of a poset and compatible morphisms to ordered pairs.
statement: A representation of a poset \(P\) in an abelian category \(\mathcal A\) is a family \(F_x\) with maps \(f_{xy}:F_x\to F_y\) for \(x\le y\), satisfying \(f_{xx}=1\) and \(f_{yz}f_{xy}=f_{xz}\). For finite \(P\) with upper-set topology this is the corresponding cellular sheaf diagram.
fate: This repeats the finite-poset construction in occurrence 1987-714.5; its elementary sheaf interpretation uses the same restriction and gluing axioms \citep[Tag 007X]{stacks2026foundations}.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, this is an established categorical encoding, with the direction fixed by the notebook's topology.

title: The abelian category of complexes and cohomology
notes: The notes introduce \(C(\mathcal A)\), bounded variants, differentials, morphisms, and \(H^i\).
statement: For an abelian category \(\mathcal A\), \(C(\mathcal A)\) has cochain complexes \((X^i,d^i)\), \(d^{i+1}d^i=0\), and degree-preserving chain maps. It is abelian with kernels and cokernels degreewise, and \(H^i(X)=\ker d^i/\operatorname{im}d^{i-1}\). The subcategories \(C^b,C^+,C^-\) impose bounded, bounded-below, or bounded-above terms.
fate: This predates the seminar; the derived-category account was already published in \citet[Chapter I]{hartshorne1966residues}. Modern definitions and cohomology are in \citet[Chapters 12--13]{stacks2026foundations}.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, these are standard definitions; cohomology need not be exact as a functor on complexes.

title: Homotopy and the quotient category
notes: A null homotopy is written \(f=d\psi+\psi d\); quotienting by such maps defines \(K(\mathcal A)\).
statement: Chain maps \(f,g:X\to Y\) are homotopic if \(f^i-g^i=d_Y^{i-1}h^i+h^{i+1}d_X^i\) for maps \(h^i:X^i\to Y^{i-1}\). Null-homotopic maps form an additive two-sided ideal. The quotient \(K(\mathcal A)\) has the same objects as \(C(\mathcal A)\), and every \(H^i\) factors through it.
fate: \citet[\S 13.8 and \S 13.11, Tag 05RR]{stacks2026foundations} gives precisely this construction; its pre-1987 setting is \citet[Chapter I]{hartshorne1966residues}.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, homotopy is weaker than isomorphism of complexes and stronger than the derived equivalence generated by quasi-isomorphisms.

title: Quasi-isomorphisms
notes: A map inducing isomorphisms in all cohomological degrees is called a quasi-isomorphism.
statement: A chain map \(f:X\to Y\) is a quasi-isomorphism if \(H^i(f)\) is an isomorphism for every integer \(i\). Such maps need not be homotopy equivalences in an arbitrary abelian category.
fate: \citet[\S 13.11, Lemma 13.11.2]{stacks2026foundations} identifies precisely this multiplicative system, in the classical derived-category construction.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the distinction from homotopy equivalence is essential and remains unchanged.

title: The Ore construction for a roof
notes: A roof with a quasi-isomorphism on one leg can be replaced by a common outgoing diagram; the construction is used to compose fractions.
statement: If \(s:Z\to X\) is a quasi-isomorphism and \(f:Z\to Y\) is a chain map, the homotopy pushout \(P=\operatorname{Cone}((s,-f):Z\to X\oplus Y)\) admits maps \(X\to P\), \(Y\to P\) commuting in \(K(\mathcal A)\), and \(Y\to P\) is a quasi-isomorphism. The dual statement uses a homotopy pullback.
reconstruction: The explicit cone and the location of the outgoing quasi-isomorphism make the diagrammatic lemma precise.
fate: This is the calculus of quasi-isomorphisms underlying \citet[Lemma 13.11.2 and \S 13.5]{stacks2026foundations}; the cone construction is classical \citep[Chapter I]{hartshorne1966residues}.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the outgoing quasi-isomorphism is on the opposite leg; commutativity is in the homotopy category.

title: The derived category as roofs
notes: Morphisms are roofs \(X\leftarrow Z\to Y\), the left map a quasi-isomorphism, modulo common refinement.
statement: For an essentially small abelian category, \(D(\mathcal A)=K(\mathcal A)[\mathrm{Qis}^{-1}]\). A morphism is represented by \(X\xleftarrow{s}Z\xrightarrow{f}Y\) with \(s\) a quasi-isomorphism. Equivalent roofs have common refinements in \(K(\mathcal A)\); composition is obtained by an Ore square. The localization is universal among functors inverting quasi-isomorphisms.
reconstruction: The size convention is stated to avoid assuming that arbitrary localization morphisms form sets.
fate: \citet[Definition 13.11.3, Tag 05RR]{stacks2026foundations}; the foundational account appears in \citet[Chapter I]{hartshorne1966residues}. Earlier companion occurrences include 1971-266.3 and 1977-438.15.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, this is the established derived-category construction; large categories require the usual universe or existence conventions.

title: Taylor telescoping and universal summation coefficients
notes: The sums \(S_r=\sum_{j=1}^n f^{(r)}(j)\) are expressed by a triangular system involving endpoint differences, with a determinant solution.
statement: For a polynomial \(f\) and an antiderivative \(F\), \[F(n+1)-F(1)=\sum_{r\ge0}\frac{S_r}{(r+1)!},\qquad f^{(p)}(n+1)-f^{(p)}(1)=\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{S_{p+r}}{r!}.\] All sums terminate, and the unit triangular system can be inverted.
reconstruction: Polynomial input supplies a rigorous domain for the notebook's formal manipulation.
fate: This is a direct polynomial version of the classical Euler--Maclaurin method. \citet[\S 2.10(i), equation 2.10.1]{nist2026dlmf} states the analytic formula with its remainder.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the polynomial identity is exact; applying an infinite Taylor expansion to an arbitrary function is unjustified.

title: Bernoulli coefficients and Euler--Maclaurin summation
notes: The universal coefficients are recovered using exponentials; the notes propose the answer for any function.
statement: Writing \(t/(e^t-1)=\sum_{r\ge0}B_rt^r/r!\), a polynomial \(f=F^{\prime}\) satisfies \[\sum_{j=1}^nf(j)=F(n+1)-F(1)+\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{B_r}{r!}\bigl(f^{(r-1)}(n+1)-f^{(r-1)}(1)\bigr).\] For nonpolynomial functions one uses a finite truncation with the Euler--Maclaurin remainder and sufficient differentiability.
reconstruction: The exact polynomial case is separated from the analytic finite-remainder theorem.
fate: \citet[equations 24.2.1 and 2.10.1]{nist2026dlmf} verifies the generating function, sign \(B_1=-1/2\), and remainder. This was classical long before 1987.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the coefficient sequence is established; the unrestricted no-remainder statement is false.

title: Symmetric-group generators and the Young-subgroup algebra
notes: The simple transpositions obey Coxeter relations; for \(H=S_k\times S_{n-k}\), the algebra consists of \(x\in\mathbb C[S_n]\) satisfying \(hx=xh=x\) for all \(h\in H\).
statement: The group \(S_n\) is generated by \(s_i=(i,i+1)\), with \(s_i^2=1\), \(s_is_j=s_js_i\) for \(|i-j|>1\), and \(s_is_{i+1}s_i=s_{i+1}s_is_{i+1}\). For \(e_H=|H|^{-1}\sum_{h\in H}h\), the displayed invariant algebra is \(e_H\mathbb C[S_n]e_H\), with unit \(e_H\); it has a basis indexed by \(H\backslash S_n/H\).
reconstruction: The averaging idempotent identifies the algebra and clarifies that its unit need not be the ambient group-algebra unit.
fate: This is the ordinary finite-group double-coset construction, related to the symmetric-group representation framework of \citet[Chapter I, \S 7]{macdonald1995symmetric}. No further theorem or unanswered question about this algebra is recorded here.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the definition is complete after making its unit explicit.

title: Truncation and a complex with one cohomology object
notes: The complex is cut off using a kernel, and, when only its zeroth cohomology survives, it is compared with that object in degree zero.
statement: If \(H^i(X)=0\) for \(i\ne0\), the canonical truncation \(\tau_{\le0}X\), with \((\tau_{\le0}X)^0=\ker d^0\), has quasi-isomorphisms \(X\leftarrow\tau_{\le0}X\to H^0(X)[0]\). Hence \(X\simeq H^0(X)[0]\) in \(D(\mathcal A)\).
fate: This is standard truncation in the derived category, already part of \citet[Chapter I]{hartshorne1966residues}; compare \citet[Chapter 13]{stacks2026foundations}.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the conclusion is canonical in the derived category and does not imply a chain-level isomorphism.

title: Cohomology objects do not generally split a complex
notes: The notes warn that several cohomology groups do not determine a complex as their direct sum, and that a splitting, when available, need not be canonical.
statement: In a general abelian category a complex need not be isomorphic in \(D(\mathcal A)\) to its graded cohomology with zero differential: the truncation triangles can have nonzero connecting extension classes. If every short exact sequence in \(\mathcal A\) splits, every complex is homotopy equivalent to its graded cohomology, although choices enter a chain-level splitting.
reconstruction: The extension-class explanation specifies the warning rather than imputing a particular example to the speaker.
fate: The distinction is built into the triangle formalism of \citet[Chapter I]{hartshorne1966residues} and \citet[\S\S 13.9--13.11]{stacks2026foundations}.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, nonformality is a real phenomenon; the semisimple hypothesis is sufficient for the stated splitting.

title: When is the homotopy category abelian?
notes: The exercise says \(K(\mathcal A)\) is abelian exactly when \(\mathcal A\) is semisimple; the handwritten explanation speaks of sums of irreducibles.
statement: For an abelian category \(\mathcal A\), \(K(\mathcal A)\) is abelian if and only if every short exact sequence in \(\mathcal A\) splits. In that case it is equivalent to the category of graded objects of \(\mathcal A\). Here semisimple means split exact; a decomposition into simple objects requires the usual additional finiteness or category hypotheses.
reconstruction: The split-exact formulation avoids silently imposing finite length. \ours{} The stated short argument is supplied in this companion.
fate: The implication from split exactness follows by splitting cycles and boundaries. Conversely an abelian triangulated category is split exact, so every morphism has a generalized inverse. For a monomorphism \(i:U\to V\) in \(\mathcal A\), apply this to its degree-zero map to obtain \(g\) with \(igi=i\); cancellation in \(\mathcal A\) gives \(gi=1_U\), forcing all exact sequences in \(\mathcal A\) to split. The triangulated structure is checked in \citet[Proposition 13.10.3]{stacks2026foundations}. Earlier occurrence 1971-266.2 discusses the general failure of abelianness.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the exercise is a settled structural criterion, with the meaning of semisimple specified.

title: Mapping cone and its elementary homotopies
notes: The cone is \(C_f^i=Y^i\oplus X^{i+1}\), but the differential is written with the reversed coordinate ordering. The cone of the identity is contractible; the cone of zero splits.
statement: For a chain map \(f:X\to Y\), put \(C_f^i=Y^i\oplus X^{i+1}\) and \(d(y,x)=(d_Yy+f(x),-d_Xx)\). Then \(C_{1_X}\) is contractible and \(C_0=Y\oplus X[1]\). If \(i:Y\to C_f\) is the inclusion, \(C_i\) is homotopy equivalent to \(X[1]\).
reconstruction: The differential has been reordered to match the declared direct sum.
fate: \citet[\S 13.9, definition and elementary cone lemmas]{stacks2026foundations} gives the standard construction. These statements were established well before the seminar \citep[Chapter I]{hartshorne1966residues}.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, all three cone properties are valid with consistent shift and summand conventions.

title: Distinguished triangles and the sign of rotation
notes: Exact triangles are those isomorphic to cone triangles, followed by a continuing sequence of shifts.
statement: The triangle \(X\xrightarrow fY\to C_f\to X[1]\), with one consistent cone convention, is distinguished; all triangles isomorphic to such ones are distinguished. If \(X\xrightarrow fY\xrightarrow gZ\xrightarrow hX[1]\) is distinguished, its rotation is \(Y\xrightarrow gZ\xrightarrow hX[1]\xrightarrow{-f[1]}Y[1]\). Its cohomology sequence is exact.
reconstruction: The negative sign on the rotated final arrow is made explicit; the notebook's continuing sequence alone does not state a sign convention.
fate: \citet[Proposition 13.10.3, proof of TR2, and equation 13.11.1.1]{stacks2026foundations} checks the rotation sign and long exact sequence. The 1966 published account predates this exposition \citep[Chapter I]{hartshorne1966residues}.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the rotation sign is indispensable even though signs can be moved by coherent changes of cone convention.

title: Complete functions of a formal alphabet
notes: For a formal sum \(P\) the coefficients \(S^r(P)\) are defined by a product generating function, with examples allowing multiplicities and differences of alphabets.
statement: For a finite alphabet with multiplicities \(P=\sum_jm_ju_j\), \(m_j\in\mathbb Z\), define \[\sum_{r\ge0}h_r[P]t^r=\prod_j(1-tu_j)^{-m_j},\qquad h_0[P]=1,\quad h_r[P]=0\ (r<0).\] Positive multiplicities give ordinary complete symmetric functions; negative ones define virtual alphabets formally.
fate: This is classical symmetric-function notation; \citet[Chapter I, \S 2]{macdonald1995symmetric}. The first edition appeared in 1979.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the construction is a formal power-series identity; no analytic convergence is required.

title: The alphabet homomorphism to triangular Toeplitz matrices
notes: The matrix \(M(P)\) has consecutive complete functions along diagonals and is called Hankel; the notes assert \(M(P+Q)=M(P)M(Q)\).
statement: Let \(M(P)_{ij}=h_{j-i}[P]\) for \(i,j\ge0\). Then \(M(P)\) is an upper triangular Toeplitz matrix with diagonal one and \(M(P+Q)=M(P)M(Q)\), since \(h_r[P+Q]=\sum_{a+b=r}h_a[P]h_b[Q]\). Every matrix entry involves a finite sum.
fate: The identity follows by multiplying the generating series in \citet[Chapter I, \S 2]{macdonald1995symmetric}. The matrix is Toeplitz, since its entries depend on the difference of the indices.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the homomorphism is correct; the notebook's matrix-name label is incorrect.

title: Cauchy--Binet through exterior powers
notes: The notes use minors of a matrix and the multiplicativity of its exterior powers.
statement: For compatible finite matrices \(A,B\), and ordered \(k\)-element index sets \(I,J\), \[\det(AB)_{I,J}=\sum_{|L|=k}\det A_{I,L}\det B_{L,J}.\] Equivalently \(\bigwedge^k(AB)=(\bigwedge^kA)(\bigwedge^kB)\); the same identity applies to the triangular matrices here because relevant sums are finite.
fate: The identity is classical multilinear algebra and underlies the determinant manipulations in \citet[Chapter I, \S\S 3--5]{macdonald1995symmetric}.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the equality is valid over every commutative coefficient ring.

title: Skew Schur functions as minors
notes: Minors of \(M(P)\), indexed by two ordered integer lists, are denoted \(S_{I\mid J}(P)\).
statement: For partitions \(\mu\subseteq\lambda\), padded to a common length \(r\), the skew Schur function is \[s_{\lambda/\mu}[P]=\det\bigl(h_{\lambda_i-\mu_j-i+j}[P]\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le r}.\] Reversing the notebook's increasing index order gives this usual partition notation.
reconstruction: The partition convention is modern; it does not replace the notebook's increasing-code convention without an index change.
fate: \citet[Chapter I, \S 5, skew Jacobi--Trudi identities]{macdonald1995symmetric}.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, these minors give the standard skew Schur functions; an explicit index reversal is necessary when comparing formulas.

title: Alternants and the Jacobi--Trudi identity
notes: The notes define Schur polynomials by a quotient of alternants and ask for the determinant identity relating this quotient to complete functions.
statement: For a partition \(\lambda\) of length at most \(n\), \[s_\lambda(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\frac{\det(x_i^{\lambda_j+n-j})}{\det(x_i^{n-j})}=\det(h_{\lambda_i-i+j}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)).\] The quotient is a symmetric polynomial with integral coefficients, since the alternating numerator is divisible by the Vandermonde.
fate: \citet[Chapter I, \S 3, equation (3.4) and historical notes]{macdonald1995symmetric} attributes the determinant identity to Jacobi.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the requested proof concerns a classical exact identity.

title: Schur coefficients and their representation meaning
notes: The text asks for explicit coefficients and a representation-theoretic interpretation; an abbreviated reference to a Gelfand--Zelevinsky 1986 paper is attached.
statement: In characteristic zero, \(s_\lambda\) is the character of the Schur functor \(S_\lambda V\) for \(\operatorname{GL}(V)\). In \(s_\lambda=\sum_\mu K_{\lambda\mu}m_\mu\), \(K_{\lambda\mu}\) counts semistandard tableaux of shape \(\lambda\) and content \(\mu\). These give a precise coefficient interpretation, though not a single factorial expression for all coefficients.
reconstruction: The coefficient basis and the polynomial representation category are supplied explicitly.
fate: The character and tableau descriptions predate 1987; \citet[Chapter I, \S 5 and Appendix A]{macdonald1995symmetric}. The notebook's terse Gelfand--Zelevinsky bibliographic pointer could not be matched securely to a particular theorem and is not used as evidence of priority.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the ordinary Schur question has an established answer; the exact intended 1986 citation remains unresolved.

title: The K-functor and Sato comparison
notes: A parenthetical passage connects the determinant formalism with a K-functor and Sato; no operator, category, or assertion is defined there.
statement: No uniquely specified mathematical statement can be recovered from this aside: neither the K-functor nor the proposed Sato correspondence is defined in the supplied pages.
fate: Targeted searches for the alphabet determinant formalism and Sato theory located related symmetric-function literature but no exact result identifiable from the fragment. The surrounding determinant identities remain independently identified.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, this is a provenance and interpretation gap, not an established unsolved theorem.

title: Plücker relations as the determinant background
notes: The note connects the identities among minors with Grassmannians and Plücker relations.
statement: For a rank-\(r\) matrix, its ordered maximal minors \(p_I\) satisfy the quadratic Pl\"ucker relations \[\sum_{a=1}^{r+1}(-1)^a p_{i_1\cdots i_{r-1}j_a}\,p_{j_1\cdots\widehat{j_a}\cdots j_{r+1}}=0,\] with each index list interpreted alternately. These are the defining equations of the Pl\"ucker embedded Grassmannian.
reconstruction: The index convention and ambient Grassmannian have been made explicit.
fate: This is the classical determinant geometry also used in \citet[\S 1]{gelfandserganova1987combinatorial}; the notebook returns to the exchange identity in record 725. The full quadratic-generation statement is explicitly recalled as classical in \citet[\S 3, opening paragraph]{speyersturmfels2003tropical}.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the relation is established; no new higher Plücker constraint is specified here.

title: Addition and multiplication of alphabets
notes: Besides the addition formula for complete functions, the notes expand a complete function of the product alphabet in products of Schur functions.
statement: For finite alphabets \(X=(x_i)\), \(Y=(y_j)\), \[h_n[X+Y]=\sum_{a+b=n}h_a[X]h_b[Y],\qquad h_n[XY]=\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}s_\lambda[X]s_\lambda[Y].\] Here \(XY\) is the alphabet \((x_iy_j)\); Schur functions with too many rows specialize to zero.
fate: \citet[Chapter I, \S 4, Cauchy identity]{macdonald1995symmetric}.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, both are exact polynomial identities, valid for virtual alphabets by formal specialization.

title: Plethysm and its Schur expansion
notes: The notes form complete functions of an alphabet whose entries are themselves monomials and write an expansion in Schur functions.
statement: For positive integers \(m,n\), \(h_n[h_m]=\sum_{\lambda\vdash mn}c_\lambda s_\lambda\), where \(c_\lambda\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) is the multiplicity of \(S_\lambda V\) in \(\operatorname{Sym}^n(\operatorname{Sym}^mV)\) in characteristic zero and sufficiently large dimension. Plethysm is defined by substitution of the eigenvalue alphabet.
reconstruction: The characteristic-zero representation interpretation explains the coefficients without claiming an explicit rule absent from the notes.
fate: \citet[Chapter I, \S 8, especially (8.2) and (8.10)]{macdonald1995symmetric}. The notes state the operation and expansion, not a quantified positivity conjecture or a uniform combinatorial rule.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the existence and nonnegativity of this expansion are classical; the fragment does not justify entering a modern plethysm open problem.

title: Flag cohomology and Schubert classes
notes: Schubert cells are compared with differential forms and a polynomial presentation of flag cohomology.
statement: For the complete flag manifold \(\operatorname{Fl}(\mathbb C^N)\), \[H^*(\operatorname{Fl}(\mathbb C^N),\mathbb Z)\simeq\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_N]/(e_1,\ldots,e_N),\qquad\deg x_i=2.\] Schubert classes form an integral basis; their indices are permutations and their complex codimensions are inversion lengths.
fate: \citet[\S\S 2--3]{bernsteingelfandgelfand1973schubert} treats the polynomial and Schubert descriptions. Its 1973 publication precedes this seminar. See earlier occurrences 1971-239.1--2 and 1985-661.3. Earlier occurrences include 1971-239.1--2 and 1985-661.1--2. The opened original note \citep[\S 4, p.~449]{lascouxschutzenberger1982schubert} explicitly recalls the integral flag quotient and Schubert basis, and the product-duality assertion following Theorem 4.3.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the cohomology is torsion free and concentrated in even real degrees.

title: Divided differences and nil-Coxeter relations
notes: The operator \(\partial_i=(1-s_i)/(x_i-x_{i+1})\) is introduced, with nilpotence, commuting, and braid relations.
statement: On \(\mathbb Z[x_1,x_2,\ldots]\), define \(\partial_if=(f-s_if)/(x_i-x_{i+1})\). Then \(\partial_i^2=0\), \(\partial_i\partial_j=\partial_j\partial_i\) for \(|i-j|>1\), and \(\partial_i\partial_{i+1}\partial_i=\partial_{i+1}\partial_i\partial_{i+1}\). If \(g\) is \(s_i\)-invariant then \(\partial_i(gf)=g\partial_if\).
fate: The divided-difference formalism appears in \citet[\S 3]{bernsteingelfandgelfand1973schubert}; the later primary Schubert-module paper recalls it in \citet[\S 1]{kraskiewiczpragacz2004schubert}. The divided-difference sequence is also recorded in 1985-661.4--8.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the operators are integral because the numerator is divisible by the displayed linear factor.

title: The Hecke deformation of the quadratic relation
notes: Alongside the nilpotent relation, the notes mention the quadratic relation \((\sigma_i+1)(\sigma_i-q)=0\) as its q-analogue.
statement: The type-A Hecke algebra is generated by \(T_i\) with braid and distant-commutation relations and \((T_i-q)(T_i+1)=0\). This is a deformation of the symmetric-group presentation at \(q=1\). The divided-difference operators themselves satisfy nilpotence and cannot satisfy this Hecke quadratic relation for generic \(q\).
reconstruction: The distinction between the nil-Coxeter operator and a Hecke generator prevents interpreting both quadratic relations simultaneously.
fate: The exact Hecke presentation is revisited in record 726 and occurs in \citet[\S 1]{kerov1987realizations}; the notebook is juxtaposing related algebras, not identifying their unchanged generators.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the analogy is valid after specifying different operators or generators.

title: Schubert polynomials from dominant codes
notes: A weakly decreasing code \(I\) is assigned the monomial \(x^I\); divided differences change adjacent entries by \((i_p,i_{p+1})\mapsto(i_{p+1},i_p-1)\) when \(i_p>i_{p+1}\).
statement: For a permutation \(w\), let \(c_i(w)=\#\{j>i:w(j)<w(i)\}\). There is a unique stable family \(\mathfrak S_w\) with \(\mathfrak S_{w_0}=x_1^{N-1}x_2^{N-2}\cdots x_{N-1}\) in \(S_N\), and \(\partial_i\mathfrak S_w=\mathfrak S_{ws_i}\) when \(\ell(ws_i)<\ell(w)\), zero otherwise. If the code is weakly decreasing, \(\mathfrak S_w=x^{c(w)}\).
reconstruction: The permutation code fixes the notebook's indexing convention.
fate: Lascoux--Sch\"utzenberger's 1982 announcement is the pre-seminar source \citep{lascouxschutzenberger1982schubert}; the definition and code convention are read in \citet[\S 1]{kraskiewiczpragacz2004schubert}. Earlier occurrence: 1985-661.7. Compare the generation from the longest permutation in 1985-661.7.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the construction is independent of a reduced word by the braid relations.

title: The worked chain from code 730 to code 025
notes: The notes compute \(Y_{730}\to Y_{702}\to Y_{062}\to Y_{025}\) using \(\partial_2,\partial_1,\partial_2\) and complete-function determinants.
statement: The divided-difference rules give \[\partial_2\partial_1\partial_2(x_1^7x_2^3)=Y_{025}=s_{(5,2)}(x_1,x_2,x_3)=h_5h_2-h_6h_1,\] where operator composition acts from right to left and each \(h_i\) uses the three-variable alphabet in the final equality.
reconstruction: \oursComputed{} The independent checks are recorded in the early-record verification log.
fate: The general rules are those of \citet[\S 1]{kraskiewiczpragacz2004schubert} and Jacobi--Trudi \citep[Chapter I, (3.4)]{macdonald1995symmetric}. The concrete equality is checked by independent symbolic polynomial expansion in the accompanying script.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the displayed example is correct after maintaining the changing alphabets in the intermediate determinants.

title: Schur functions as special Schubert polynomials
notes: For an increasing code \(0\le i_1\le\cdots\le i_n\) followed by zeroes, the notes identify \(Y_I\) with the Schur function previously defined.
statement: If a permutation is Grassmannian with its only possible descent at \(n\), then \(\mathfrak S_w=s_\lambda(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\), where \(\lambda=(c_n(w),\ldots,c_1(w))\). Equivalently its first \(n\) code entries are weakly increasing and the later entries zero.
fate: This is a classical specialization of the Schubert construction, recalled in \citet[\S 1]{kraskiewiczpragacz2004schubert} and originating in the Lascoux--Sch\"utzenberger theory \citep{lascouxschutzenberger1982schubert}.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the identity explains why the previous worked example ends at an ordinary Schur function.

title: The finite Schubert basis and its cardinality
notes: For \(n+1\) variables, codes satisfy \(0\le i_1\le n,\ldots,0\le i_{n+1}\le0\); the notes then give the dimension as \(n!\), despite listing six elements for \(n=2\).
statement: For \(R_N=\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_N]/(e_1,\ldots,e_N)\), the classes \(\mathfrak S_w\), \(w\in S_N\), form a free integral basis, hence \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Z}R_N=N!\). In the notebook's \(N=n+1\) convention the count is \((n+1)!\). Stable Schubert polynomials indexed by permutations outside \(S_N\), specialized to these variables, vanish in this quotient.
fate: The flag-cohomology basis is classical \citep[\S\S 2--3]{bernsteingelfandgelfand1973schubert}. The count also follows independently by multiplying the \((n+1),n,\ldots,1\) choices for the code. The opened original note \citep[\S 4, p.~449]{lascouxschutzenberger1982schubert} explicitly recalls the integral flag quotient and Schubert basis, and the product-duality assertion following Theorem 4.3.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the basis assertion is correct; the printed factorial loses one in its argument.

title: The symmetric-group action in the Schubert basis
notes: Gelfand asks how variable permutation by \(S_n\) is written in Schubert polynomials.
statement: The action on the coinvariant algebra is determined by \[s_i[P]=[P]-(x_i-x_{i+1})[\partial_iP].\] Thus apply \(\partial_i\mathfrak S_w\), multiply by the indicated linear form, and reduce in the finite Schubert basis. Over \(\mathbb Q\), the ungraded coinvariant representation is the regular representation of \(S_N\).
reconstruction: The quotient, the rational coefficient field for the regular representation, and the algorithmic meaning of an explicit formula are specified.
fate: The Weyl-group action on flag cohomology is already a subject of \citet[\S 3]{bernsteingelfandgelfand1973schubert}. The displayed operator formula follows immediately from the definition, so the recorded request is computational exposition rather than an unresolved existence problem.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the action is explicit; the graded pieces are not each regular representations.
speaker: I. M. Gelfand

title: Poincaré pairing and adjoint divided differences
notes: The pairing is obtained from \(\partial_1\partial_2\partial_1(PQ)\) in three variables; divided differences are self-adjoint, and a code-complement rule gives the dual basis.
statement: On the coinvariant algebra for \(S_N\), define \((P,Q)=\epsilon(\partial_{w_0}(PQ))\), where \(\epsilon\) sets all variables to zero. Then \((\partial_iP,Q)=(P,\partial_iQ)\). With the standard Schubert indexing, \((\mathfrak S_u,\mathfrak S_v)=\delta_{v,w_0u}\); equivalently \(c_i(v)=N-i-c_i(u)\).
reconstruction: The augmentation and indexing convention clarify the notebook's phrase that the answer is a number in the quotient. \oursComputed{} The independent checks are recorded in the early-record verification log.
fate: The pairing is integration on the flag manifold and the operators are its push-pull operators \citep[\S 3]{bernsteingelfandgelfand1973schubert}. A separate finite-rank polynomial check tests the code complement and the adjoint identity. The opened original note \citep[\S 4, p.~449]{lascouxschutzenberger1982schubert} explicitly recalls the integral flag quotient and Schubert basis, and the product-duality assertion following Theorem 4.3.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the pairing is perfect over the integers, and evaluation after the longest divided difference is necessary for arbitrary degrees.

title: Freeness over symmetric polynomials
notes: The polynomial ring in three variables is said to be free over its symmetric subring with Schubert-polynomial basis.
statement: For \(N\ge1\), \(\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_N]\) is a free module over \(\mathbb Z[e_1,\ldots,e_N]\), with basis \(\{\mathfrak S_w:w\in S_N\}\). The basis has \(N!\) elements; it is not the entire stable family indexed by all finite permutations.
fate: This is the polynomial form of the coinvariant-basis theorem \citep[\S 3]{bernsteingelfandgelfand1973schubert}; the modern Schubert convention is fixed in \citet[\S 1]{kraskiewiczpragacz2004schubert}.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the integral freeness statement holds with the finite indexing set made explicit.

title: Schubert polynomials as characters
notes: Gelfand requests a generalization of character theory whose characters are Schubert functions; the line also mentions irreducible representations without naming a group or category.
statement: For each finite permutation \(w\), one can construct a finite-dimensional cyclic polynomial module \(S_w(E_\bullet)\) for the triangular group preserving a complete flag, whose diagonal-torus character is \(\mathfrak S_w\). It is generally not irreducible. A nonsymmetric Schubert polynomial cannot be the character of a polynomial \(\operatorname{GL}_N\)-representation, whose torus character is symmetric.
reconstruction: The representation category is supplied by the matched theorem; irreducibility is explicitly not imported into it.
fate: \citet[Theorem 4.1]{kraskiewiczpragacz2004schubert} proves the exact Borel-module realization. Its introduction dates the preprint to 1986 and its announcement to 1987; the full article appeared in 2004. Thus this is class E at the seminar date, not a 2004 solution of a new 1987 problem. Related occurrence 1985-661.3 concerns Schubert polynomial representatives, not this character-realization question.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the character realization is established in the Borel category; the notebook does not identify a category supporting its extra irreducibility wording.
speaker: I. M. Gelfand

title: A theory organizing determinant formulas
notes: In discussing Muir's determinant books, Gelfand proposes building a theory behind the formulas, by analogy with integrable systems.
statement: The remark specifies neither a class of determinant identities, an invariant, nor a proposed equivalence. It supports a research programme, but no uniquely quantified conjecture or theorem.
fate: The adjacent Schur and Schubert identities have exact classical matches. Searches for the Muir and integrable-system connection do not turn this unspecific sentence into a definite outstanding problem.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the programme remains too broad for a mathematical fate classification beyond F.

title: Double categories and the interchange law
notes: The heading says 2-categories, while the data comprise objects, horizontal arrows, vertical arrows, and squares with two compositions.
statement: A strict double category is a category object in categories: its squares have horizontal and vertical boundary arrows and associative unital compositions \(\circ_h,\circ_v\) satisfying \[(A\circ_vB)\circ_h(C\circ_vD)=(A\circ_hC)\circ_v(B\circ_hD)\] whenever the four squares have matching boundaries.
reconstruction: The modern name separates this structure from the strict 2-category in the later intervention.
fate: \citet[\S 1, equations (1.1)--(1.5)]{brownspencer1976double} provides these exact four kinds of data and the interchange law; the paper appeared in 1976.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, this is established double-category terminology; the notebook uses a broader informal label.

title: Why naive corner-index contraction fails interchange
notes: Four-index tensors are multiplied by contracting the two indices on a common edge; the note says this example does not satisfy interchange.
statement: Write a square tensor as \(A(k,l;i,j)\). Define horizontal contraction by \((A\circ_hC)(k,r;i,s)=\sum_{j,l}A(k,l;i,j)C(l,r;j,s)\), and vertical contraction by \((A\circ_vB)(k,l;u,v)=\sum_{i,j}A(k,l;i,j)B(i,j;u,v)\). With indices \(0,1\), take the only nonzero entries of \(A,C,B,D\) to be, respectively, \(A(0,0;0,0)=C(0,0;0,0)=B(0,1;0,0)=D(1,0;0,0)=1\). The outer all-zero entry of \((A\circ_hC)\circ_v(B\circ_hD)\) is 1, while that of \((A\circ_vB)\circ_h(C\circ_vD)\) is 0.
reconstruction: The full vertical contraction convention and sparse counterexample are ours; the notebook gives only a drawing of vertical composition. \oursComputed{} The independent checks are recorded in the early-record verification log.
fate: The failure follows by two direct finite contractions, independently checked in the accompanying script. The relevant required axiom is \citet[equation (1.5)]{brownspencer1976double}.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the proposed naive contraction does fail; suitable categorical tensor constructions must keep different boundary data.

title: Strict two-categories and Cat
notes: Kontsevich proposes morphisms between morphisms with identical endpoints; Cat is the example. The note calls this a special case obtained by collapsing vertical arrows.
statement: A strict 2-category has objects, 1-morphisms, and 2-morphisms between parallel 1-morphisms, with strictly associative unital horizontal and vertical compositions satisfying interchange. In \(\mathrm{Cat}\), these are categories, functors, and natural transformations. A strict 2-category embeds as a double category whose vertical arrows are identities.
fate: This is pre-1987 higher-category formalism; \citet[\S 1 and references to B\'enabou, Gray, and Kelly--Street]{brownspencer1976double} distinguishes the double-category structure and its specializations.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the two descriptions are related, but their general definitions are not interchangeable.
speaker: M. L. Kontsevich

title: Harmonic boundary data as a categorical suggestion
notes: Gelfand draws a square with \(\Delta u=0\), records \(u\) and \(\partial u/\partial n\) on its boundary, and asks Keldysh, Chentsov, and Gelfand to consider the idea.
statement: The data suggest composing boundary-value relations by gluing domains. No spaces of admissible Cauchy data, corner conditions, morphisms, or composition law are defined, so an exact double-category theorem cannot be extracted.
fate: The boundary-value and categorical keywords were checked against the surrounding record and the later higher-category thread. No precise publication can be matched to this fragment without choosing new analytic definitions.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, this is a mathematically motivated programme but an indeterminate statement, not an identified unsolved analytic problem.
speaker: I. M. Gelfand

title: Homotopy squares of a filtered space
notes: For \(X_0\subset X_1\subset X\), vertices lie in \(X_0\), edges are paths in \(X_1\), and squares map \((I^2,\partial I^2)\) to \((X,X_1)\), modulo homotopy.
statement: For a filtered space \(X_0\subset X_1\subset X\), take paths in \(X_1\) with endpoints in \(X_0\), and squares in \(X\) whose edges lie in \(X_1\) and vertices in \(X_0\). Homotopies must preserve these filtrations and fix vertices; the resulting homotopy double-groupoid construction has horizontal and vertical gluing. At a basepoint, its relative structure is encoded by the crossed module \(\pi_2(X,X_1)\to\pi_1(X_1)\).
reconstruction: The filtered and vertex-fixed homotopy conventions are essential additions to the shorthand.
fate: \citet[\S 1, Example 1; introduction; Theorem A]{brownspencer1976double} explains squares, their double compositions, and the crossed-module relation. Theorem A circulated in a 1972 preliminary report, before its 1976 publication.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the construction is classical once the homotopies and connections are specified; arbitrary unrelative homotopy would not preserve the necessary boundary data.

title: The cone lemma with its outgoing quasi-isomorphism
notes: The initial roof has \(Z\to X\) a quasi-isomorphism; the outgoing diagram labels \(X\to Z_1\), rather than \(Y\to Z_1\), as a quasi-isomorphism.
statement: For \(Z\xrightarrow{s}X\), \(Z\xrightarrow fY\), with \(s\) a quasi-isomorphism, there is a homotopy-commutative square with \(X\to P\) and a quasi-isomorphism \(Y\to P\). One may take \(P=\operatorname{Cone}((s,-f):Z\to X\oplus Y)\).
fate: This repeats occurrence 1987-717.5 and the established multiplicative-system construction \citep[Lemma 13.11.2 and \S 13.5]{stacks2026foundations}. The wrong-leg version cannot be true for \(s=1_Z\) and an arbitrary map \(f\).
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the correct lemma holds in the homotopy category; the original diagram requires an emendation.

title: Homotopies, localization, and refinement of roofs
notes: The page repeats \(f^i=dg^i+g^{i+1}d\), inverts quasi-isomorphisms in \(K(\mathcal A)\), and generates equivalence of roofs by precomposing with a quasi-isomorphism.
statement: With complexes as objects, \(C(\mathcal A)\to K(\mathcal A)\to D(\mathcal A)\) first identifies homotopic chain maps and then inverts every quasi-isomorphism. A roof \((s,f)\) is equivalent to \((s\chi,f\chi)\) for a quasi-isomorphism \(\chi:Z_1\to Z\); the equivalence relation generated by these refinements is the derived-morphism relation.
fate: \citet[Definition 13.11.3 and localization construction]{stacks2026foundations}; compare occurrences 1987-717.3--6 and earlier 1971-266.3.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, this is a repeated foundational construction rather than a new problem or later development.

title: The two-sided Bernoulli shift and baker map
notes: The notes depict a bi-infinite sequence of zeroes and ones and encode the two halves as binary coordinates of a square.
statement: Let \(\Sigma=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb Z}\) with product measure and \((\sigma a)_j=a_{j+1}\). Set \(x=.a_0a_1\cdots\), \(y=.a_{-1}a_{-2}\cdots\). Outside the null set of ambiguous dyadic expansions, this gives a measure-preserving conjugacy with \[B(x,y)=(2x-\lfloor2x\rfloor,(y+\lfloor2x\rfloor)/2).\]
reconstruction: The formula, probability measure, and dyadic exception are supplied explicitly.
fate: The coding is checked directly by moving the binary point. The shift and hyperbolic examples belong to the pre-1987 theory surveyed in \citet[hyperbolic examples]{smale1967dynamical}; only that survey's metadata was reopened in this run.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the measure-theoretic conjugacy is exact almost everywhere; the square and the Cantor product are not globally homeomorphic.

title: Finite observation and loss of predictive information
notes: Iterating the shift is described as gradually losing information about a point when only finitely many digits are known.
statement: For independent fair binary coordinates, if only \(a_j\) with \(|j|\le m\) are observed, then any unobserved coordinate \(a_k\), \(|k|>m\), still has conditional probabilities \(1/2,1/2\). Under \(\sigma^n\), the observed window shifts, and future digits outside the initial finite window are not determined by it. The complete two-sided shift remains invertible.
reconstruction: Conditional probability is our precise interpretation of the informal information claim.
fate: This precise finite-window statement is a direct consequence of product independence, not a new theorem about destruction of exact state information. It clarifies the standard symbolic-dynamics example associated with \citet{smale1967dynamical}.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the observation-level assertion is correct; exact invertible dynamics does not erase its full initial data.

title: Negative curvature as a geometric hyperbolicity example
notes: The closing line compares the binary example with geodesics on a negatively curved manifold.
statement: If \(M\) is a closed smooth Riemannian manifold with strictly negative sectional curvature, its geodesic flow on the unit tangent bundle is Anosov: the tangent bundle splits into flow, stable, and unstable subbundles with uniform exponential contraction in forward or backward time.
reconstruction: The closed-manifold hypothesis and the exact hyperbolicity assertion supply a limited rigorous interpretation.
fate: \citet{anosov1967geodesic} is the original 1967 monograph; its Math-Net publication record was opened. The notebook does not state a literal conjugacy of this flow to a binary shift.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, uniform hyperbolicity holds under compactness and negative curvature; arbitrary noncompact negatively curved manifolds need additional uniformity conditions.

title: Smooth conjugacy of circle diffeomorphisms to rotations
notes: Gelfand says the circle-conjugacy question is nontrivial and names Denjoy, Arnold, and Herman.
statement: An orientation-preserving \(C^2\) circle diffeomorphism with irrational rotation number is topologically conjugate to the corresponding rotation. If it is \(C^\infty\) and its rotation number satisfies a Diophantine condition \(|\alpha-p/q|\ge Cq^{-2-\nu}\) for some \(C,\nu>0\) and all rational \(p/q\), the conjugacy can be chosen \(C^\infty\). Smoothness alone does not ensure a smooth conjugacy for every irrational rotation number.
reconstruction: The modern formulation separates topological and smooth conjugacy, which the notes do not spell out.
fate: \citet[Introduction and main theorem]{yoccoz1984conjugaison} proves the smooth Diophantine statement, generalizing Herman, in 1984. It predates this intervention.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the regularity and arithmetic qualifications are essential; the remark is about an established theory, not an explicitly new conjecture.

title: Representations on sets of intermediate Hausdorff dimension
notes: Gelfand asks for a representation theory of infinite discrete groups on functions on sets of intermediate Hausdorff dimension, suggesting that some classical theory might reappear.
statement: The fragment specifies no class of groups, fractal spaces, measures, function spaces, actions, or meaning of recovering the classical theory. Consequently there is no definite universal existence or classification statement to test.
fate: Targeted searches for Gelfand, representations of discrete groups, and Hausdorff dimension found related boundary and fractal representation constructions, but no publication with the quantifiers of an identifiable question here. Those thematic developments are not treated as a solution.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the programme remains indeterminate from this record; F records the missing formulation and does not assert that no such representations exist.

title: A point outside short intervals around the rationals
notes: The school-level question covers the nth rational by an interval of length \(\varepsilon/2^n\) and asks for a number left uncovered.
statement: For any enumeration \((q_n)_{n\ge1}\) of \(\mathbb Q\) and open intervals \(I_n\ni q_n\) with \(|I_n|=\varepsilon2^{-n}\), \(m(\bigcup_nI_n)\le\varepsilon\). Hence for \(0<\varepsilon<1\), \([0,1]\setminus\bigcup_nI_n\) has measure at least \(1-\varepsilon\), is nonempty, and consists of irrationals. A particular uncovered number depends on the chosen enumeration and intervals.
reconstruction: The unit interval and epsilon bound turn the informal task into a precise existence assertion.
fate: This is countable subadditivity of Lebesgue measure, explicitly reconstructed here. The basic measure setting is described in \citet[\S 2.5]{hutchinson1981fractals}; no fixed numerical example can be inferred without the missing interval data.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the existence claim is elementary; the source does not specify enough data to name one universal uncovered real number.

title: Hausdorff dimension of the Cantor set
notes: Gelfand asks for the Hausdorff dimension of the perfect Cantor set, without spelling out its construction.
statement: For the middle-thirds Cantor set \(C\), defined by \(C=\tfrac13C\cup(\tfrac23+\tfrac13C)\), \(\dim_HC=\log2/\log3\), and its Hausdorff measure in that dimension is finite and positive. An arbitrary perfect nowhere-dense subset of the line need not have this dimension.
reconstruction: Middle thirds is the conventional interpretation, explicitly marked because the page only says Cantor perfect set.
fate: \citet[\S 5.3(1), with the examples in \S 3.3]{hutchinson1981fractals} gives the self-similar dimension theorem. The paper appeared as a 1979 ANU report before its 1981 publication; this particular Cantor dimension is older still.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the standard middle-thirds exercise is settled; the construction must be specified to make the answer unique.
speaker: I. M. Gelfand

title: Squaring and one-sided binary dynamics
notes: For \(z\mapsto z^2\), the unit circle is invariant, the inside tends to zero, the outside to infinity, and the circle map resembles the one-sided baker map.
statement: If \(|z|<1\), \(z^{2^n}\to0\); if \(|z|>1\), it tends to infinity on the Riemann sphere. On \(z=e^{2\pi i\theta}\), iteration is \(\theta\mapsto2\theta\pmod1\). Binary coding gives the one-sided shift apart from dyadic ambiguity; this map is two-to-one, unlike the invertible two-sided baker transformation.
fate: The formulas follow directly from exponentiation. This same base example introduces \citet[p.~401]{sullivan1985quasiconformal}.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the dynamics is completely explicit and the one-sided qualifier is mathematically significant.

title: The Fatou set and the Julia set
notes: The Fatou set is the open set of local normality of the iterates, and its closed complement is the Julia set; the family is called compact.
statement: For a rational map \(R:\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}\) of degree at least two, \(F(R)\) consists of points with a neighborhood on which \(\{R^n:n\ge0\}\) is normal for locally uniform convergence in the spherical metric. \(J(R)=\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus F(R)\) is closed. Normal means relative sequential compactness in this topology, not that the set of iterates is itself closed and compact.
fate: \citet[p.~403]{sullivan1985quasiconformal} states this stable-set definition and its relation to Fatou's normal-family formulation.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, these are the standard definitions with the spherical topology specified.

title: An empty Fatou set requires the rational-map setting
notes: The notes say the normality set may be empty, after beginning with polynomials and allowing rational functions more generally.
statement: A rational map of degree at least two can have \(F(R)=\varnothing\), for example a Latt\`es map induced by an expanding endomorphism of an elliptic curve. A polynomial of degree at least two always has a nonempty basin of infinity and therefore a nonempty Fatou set.
reconstruction: The rational-versus-polynomial qualification is supplied explicitly; the example identifies the standard scope.
fate: The distinction is between the two ambient classes named in the record. The rational setting of \citet[Introduction]{sullivan1985quasiconformal} permits empty stable set; the polynomial exception follows from growth outside a sufficiently large disk.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the assertion is valid for rational maps, not for all maps in the narrower polynomial subcase.

title: Sullivan: no wandering Fatou components
notes: Sullivan is credited with showing that every component orbit stabilizes and that there are finitely many fixed components.
statement: For every rational map \(R\) of degree at least two and every Fatou component \(U\), there exist integers \(m\ge0,p\ge1\) such that \(R^{m+p}(U)=R^m(U)\). There are finitely many periodic component cycles. Eventual periodicity does not mean that every component eventually becomes fixed under \(R\).
fate: \citet[Theorem 1, p.~404]{sullivan1985quasiconformal} states eventual periodicity exactly; the following discussion treats the finite periodic types. The article appeared in September 1985, before the seminar.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the no-wandering-domain theorem is established; replacing periodic cycles by eventual fixed points overstates it.

title: The quasiconformal deformation argument
notes: The proof sketch supposes an infinite orbit of components and changes the conformal structures while keeping the map conformal.
statement: The strategy is to assign compatible Beltrami data along a hypothetical wandering orbit, integrate it by the measurable Riemann mapping theorem, and obtain too many independent quasiconformal deformations for the finite-dimensional space of rational maps of the fixed degree. Producing the independent deformations and controlling conjugacy is part of the proof, not a consequence of parameter counting alone.
fate: \citet[\S\S 7--10]{sullivan1985quasiconformal} implements the method. The introduction dates earlier lectures to 1978, 1980--81, and 1981; the final article is 1985.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the notebook accurately signals the proof mechanism but does not record a complete proof.

title: The area of a disk-packing residual set
notes: A square filled with successively smaller tangent disks is drawn, with the instruction to inscribe them and prove that the remainder has measure zero.
statement: Given a specified countable family of disjoint open disks \(D_j\subset Q\), the proposed conclusion would be \(m_2(Q\setminus\bigcup_jD_j)=0\). The notebook does not specify how the disks are chosen, which gaps must be filled, or a maximality or uniformity condition. Disjointness alone allows a positive-area remainder.
fate: The scan shows only a tangency sketch and the word \ru{вписываем}. Searches for residual disk packings distinguish Apollonian and arbitrary packings; their theorems have different hypotheses. None can be identified as this exact unstated algorithm.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the intended packing process is indeterminate; no general zero-area theorem is asserted on the available data.

title: The dimension of the same packing remainder
notes: The second question asks for Hausdorff dimension strictly below two.
statement: For \(K=Q\setminus\bigcup_jD_j\), the requested claim is \(\dim_HK<2\). Even the additional condition \(m_2(K)=0\) would not imply it: zero measure and strict dimension deficit are different properties. The missing disk-selection rule prevents a uniquely specified conjecture.
fate: No exact packing algorithm or quantitative scaling assumption was found in the supplied page or matched by targeted literature searches. Self-similar dimension results such as \citet[\S 5.3]{hutchinson1981fractals} require contraction data absent here.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the strict dimension bound cannot be classified as a definite open or solved problem without the omitted construction.

title: Vector matroids and symmetric basis exchange
notes: The independent subfamilies of a finite vector configuration define its matroid. A displayed axiom permits simultaneous exchange in two bases.
statement: Let \(E\) be finite. A nonempty family \(\mathcal B\) of equal-cardinality subsets is a matroid basis family if, for \(B_1,B_2\in\mathcal B\) and \(y\in B_2\setminus B_1\), there exists \(x\in B_1\setminus B_2\) such that both \(B_1-x+y\) and \(B_2-y+x\) belong to \(\mathcal B\). This symmetric exchange formulation is equivalent to the usual basis axiom. For a vector configuration, the bases are its maximal independent subfamilies.
reconstruction: Nonemptiness, equal cardinality, and exclusion of the exchanged element from the other basis are explicit.
fate: This is classical matroid theory; the representation and independence definitions are stated in \citet[Theorem 1.6 and \S 1]{oxleybriefly}, while the basis-based bimatroid reformulation is recalled in \citet[Proposition 2.2]{rohrleulirsch2026bimatroids}. It repeats the subject of occurrence 1985-658.12.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the finite nonempty-family and equal-cardinality conventions make the displayed axiom precise.

title: The Fano configuration and characteristic two
notes: The seven-point diagram is to be realized over \(\mathbb F_2\), but not over \(\mathbb R\) or \(\mathbb C\).
statement: The rank-three Fano matroid \(F_7\), whose lines are the dependent triples in \(\mathbb F_2^3\setminus\{0\}\), is representable over a field \(k\) if and only if \(\operatorname{char}k=2\). In particular its seven indicated incidence relations cannot all arise from a rank-three real or complex vector configuration with that matroid.
fate: \citet[Theorem 4.1]{oxleybriefly} states the exact field criterion. The seven nonzero binary vectors give the recorded realization. This is the same exercise as 1985-658.14.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the problem is settled and is an expository obstruction to representability over the specified fields.

title: Which finite matroids are real or complex representable?
notes: The notebook calls the general question of representability over \(\mathbb R\) or \(\mathbb C\) unsolved, without specifying a type of classification.
statement: For a finite rank-\(r\) matroid on \([n]\) with basis list \(\mathcal B\), representability over \(k=\mathbb R\) or \(\mathbb C\) is equivalent to the existence of \(A\in k^{r\times n}\) satisfying \(\det A_B\ne0\) for \(B\in\mathcal B\), and \(\det A_I=0\) for every other \(r\)-subset \(I\). These are finitely many polynomial conditions, and their solvability is decidable over both fields.
reconstruction: The finite-input decision interpretation is made explicit; it is not claimed to supply an efficient or illuminating combinatorial classification.
fate: \citet[\S 2, pp.~15--42, and \S 3, pp.~43--46]{tarski1951decision} explicitly states quantifier elimination over the reals and its complex extension. The nonvanishing conditions can equivalently be encoded by an auxiliary equation \(u\prod_{B\in\mathcal B}\det A_B=1\). Thus the finite decision problem was settled before 1987. Occurrences 1985-658.13 and 1985-658.16 already connect representability with polynomial systems.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, a finite decision procedure exists; the source specifies no stronger structural classification or complexity target that could responsibly be declared open.

title: Matroids representable over every field
notes: The notes say that representability over every field has been characterized.
statement: For a finite matroid \(M\), the following are equivalent: \(M\) is representable over every field; \(M\) has a totally unimodular real matrix representation; and \(M\) has no minor isomorphic to \(U_{2,4}\), \(F_7\), or \(F_7^*\). Such matroids are called regular.
fate: \citet[Lemma 4.4 and Theorem 4.5]{oxleybriefly} gives the exact equivalences and attributes them to Tutte 1958. The original Tutte paper was located but could not be opened in this run; the checked modern author exposition is therefore the immediate evidence.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the statement is an established characterization, with no new 1987 question recorded.

title: The bimatroid of nonzero minors
notes: For a matrix with row set \(E\) and column set \(F\), the notes retain all pairs of equally sized subsets indexing a nonzero minor.
statement: For a matrix \(A\in k^{E\times F}\), define \(\mathcal R(A)=\{(I,J):I\subseteq E,\ J\subseteq F,\ |I|=|J|,\ \det A_{I,J}\ne0\}\), including \((\varnothing,\varnothing)\) with determinant one. This records joint row-column dependence at every size, rather than just the row and column matroids.
fate: \citet[Example 2.3]{rohrleulirsch2026bimatroids} gives this exact definition and recalls its origin in \citet{kung1978bimatroids}, published in 1978. The latter original remained inaccessible, so its attribution is indirect; the former result was read.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the construction was established before this seminar and has an exact distinguished-basis matroid encoding.

title: An axiom system for bimatroids
notes: The explicit question asks for axioms on the collection of nonzero square minors.
statement: For finite disjoint \(E,F\), a collection \(\mathcal R\) of pairs \((I,J)\) with \(|I|=|J|\) is an abstract bimatroid exactly when \(\{(E\setminus I)\sqcup J:(I,J)\in\mathcal R\}\) is a matroid basis family on \(E\sqcup F\) containing \(E\). Thus nonemptiness, the pair \((\varnothing,\varnothing)\), and the ordinary basis-exchange axiom after this substitution are a complete axiom system. In the matrix case the extended matroid is represented by \([I_E\mid A]\).
fate: \citet[Proposition 2.2 and Example 2.3]{rohrleulirsch2026bimatroids} proves this equivalence in the exposition of Kung's 1978 theory. This is a later checked source for an older answer, not a 2026 solution date.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026, the recorded axiomatization problem is solved by an explicit exchange system; abstract bimatroids need not be realizable matrices.

title: The comparison with the uncertain named bimatroid theory
notes: The page asks how a bimatroid notion in Gelfand--Serganova, UMN, relates to a name transcribed tentatively as \ru{Кунтом}.
statement: An exact comparison would require two specified definitions and a map between their objects. The named passage in Gelfand--Serganova and the second surname are not identified unambiguously by the record. Kung is a plausible bibliographic lead, but this cannot determine the missing first definition.
fate: The full English text of \citet{gelfandserganova1987combinatorial} was opened and searched; it develops ordinary and Coxeter matroids, but no occurrence of bimatroid identified the intended definition. \citet{kung1978bimatroids} is a relevant 1978 lead, with its modern formulation checked in \citet{rohrleulirsch2026bimatroids}. Neither fact proves the requested equivalence.
