title: Primary fields, descendants and conformal families
notes: Primaries satisfy \(L_n\phi=\bar L_n\phi=0\) for \(n>0\), \(L_0\phi=h\phi,\bar L_0\phi=\bar h\phi\), with \(h,\bar h\ge0\); the algebra is written as a direct sum of their descendant families.
statement: At the origin a highest-weight state has the displayed annihilation and eigenvalue conditions. Applying negative modes generates its highest-weight module, with null states quotiented out in an irreducible unitary family. In a unitary positive-energy theory \(h,\bar h\ge0\). A direct sum of such families requires an appropriate discrete semisimple spectrum; it is not automatic for every conformal theory or every noncompact model.
reconstruction: Coordinate origin, null-state quotient and the conditions for a direct-sum decomposition are supplied.
fate: \citet[Section~3, equations~(3.8)--(3.13)]{belavinpolyakovzamolodchikov1984infinite} presents primary fields and conformal families. The result predates this lecture.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: Standard within the stated unitary highest-weight framework. The algebraic direct-sum sentence needs spectral/semisimplicity hypotheses, and the source does not pose a new singular-vector classification problem.

title: Scaling weights, spin and the identity field
notes: The identity has weights zero. Under \(z\mapsto\lambda z,\bar z\mapsto\bar\lambda z\), the notes assign the primary the factor \(\lambda^h\bar\lambda^{\bar h}\) and call \(h-\bar h\) its spin.
statement: The second coordinate must be \(\bar z\mapsto\bar\lambda\bar z\). For a primary, \(h+\bar h\) is its scaling dimension and \(h-\bar h\) its spin. In a passive coordinate-change convention \(\phi_{\rm new}(\lambda z,\bar\lambda\bar z)=\lambda^{-h}\bar\lambda^{-\bar h}\phi(z,\bar z)\); active conventions reverse this placement. The identity has \((h,\bar h)=(0,0)\).
reconstruction: The missing coordinate conjugation is a literal error; the sign of the transformation factor is a convention that the source leaves unstated.
fate: \citet[Introduction, equations~(1.16)--(1.17); Section~3]{belavinpolyakovzamolodchikov1984infinite} gives these transformation laws and weights.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: Established after correcting the missing bar and specifying the active/passive convention. No sign correction of the weight factor is imposed without that convention.

title: An angle invariant for a line and a plane in three dimensions
notes: The preamble calls an angle a complete orbit invariant and asks for its attainable values. Problem 1 asks for the angle between a line and a plane in three-dimensional space, explicitly separating intersecting and nonintersecting cases.
statement: For an affine line \(\ell\) and an affine plane H under all Euclidean isometries, the direction angle \(\alpha\in[0,\pi/2]\), together with their distance \(\delta\ge0\), is complete, with the restriction \(\alpha>0\Rightarrow\delta=0\). When \(\alpha=0\), delta distinguishes a contained line from a disjoint parallel line. For linear subspaces only \(\delta=0\) occurs. Under origin-preserving orthogonal maps alone, additional positional data are needed for affine objects.
reconstruction: Allowing translations is an explicit interpretation of the nonintersecting case, not an unannounced change from the preamble about orthogonal maps.
fate: The directional angle is the elementary case of the singular-value characterization in \citet[Section~3, Theorem~1]{bjorckgolub1973angles}. The affine distance correction follows directly by moving the closest point or intersection to the origin.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: Classical and solved after fixing the acting group. An angle alone is not a complete invariant of disjoint affine configurations.

title: An angle invariant for two planes in three dimensions
notes: Problem 2 asks for the angle between two planes in three-dimensional space.
statement: For linear two-planes U,W in \(\mathbb R^3\), their two principal angles are \(0,\theta\), with \(0\le\theta\le\pi/2\); theta is the acute angle between their normal lines and is a complete O(3) invariant. If affine planes are intended, distinct parallel planes additionally require their distance \(\delta>0\); nonparallel planes intersect, and their sole nonzero directional angle suffices under Euclidean isometries.
reconstruction: The linear and affine interpretations are separated.
fate: The linear statement is a dimension-three case of \citet[Section~3, Theorem~1]{bjorckgolub1973angles}. The affine supplement is elementary and is needed because the immediately preceding task includes disjoint affine objects.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: Solved classical exercise. The source should not be read as claiming that one scalar classifies every origin-dependent affine placement.

title: Two principal angles classify two planes in four dimensions
notes: Problem 3 repeats the question about two two-dimensional subspaces of a four-dimensional inner-product space, without choosing coordinate axes.
statement: The complete O(4) invariant is \(0\le\theta_1\le\theta_2\le\pi/2\), with cosines the singular values of the cross-Gram matrix of orthonormal frames. Every such pair is realized by \(U=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2)\) and \(W=\operatorname{span}(\cos\theta_1e_1+\sin\theta_1e_3,\cos\theta_2e_2+\sin\theta_2e_4)\).
fate: \citet[Section~3, Theorem~1]{bjorckgolub1973angles} gives the established singular-value formulation. This is the exact recurrence of 1987-735.2, with the range request supplied by the problem-sheet preamble.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: Solved, including the full range of attainable invariants. The treatment for SO(4) requires the separate orientation discussion below.

title: A vector and a subspace require magnitude as well as direction
notes: Problem 4 gives \(v\in L\), a k-dimensional subspace V, and an inner product on the n-dimensional space L; it asks for their angle.
statement: Under O(L), a pair (v,V) is classified by \(n,k,\|P_Vv\|,\|P_{V^\perp}v\|\). For \(v\ne0\), these are equivalently the norm of v and the angle \(\alpha\) defined by \(\cos\alpha=\|P_Vv\|/\|v\|\). Every pair of nonnegative component norms is possible when \(0<k<n\); if k=0 the first is zero, and if k=n the second is zero. The zero vector is a separate orbit with no direction angle.
reconstruction: The source does not require a unit vector; its length is therefore retained.
fate: The projection formula is the rank-one case of \citet[Section~3]{bjorckgolub1973angles}; completeness follows by independently rotating the two orthogonal components.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: Solved. The problem-sheet definition of a complete invariant makes normalization material: angle alone does not distinguish vectors of different lengths.

title: Finite-dimensional pairs: complete invariants and their exact range
notes: Problem 5 asks for the angle between subspaces V,W of dimensions k,m in an n-dimensional inner-product space.
statement: Let \(r=\min(k,m)\) and \(q=\max(0,k+m-n)\). The ordered principal angles \(0\le\theta_1\le\cdots\le\theta_r\le\pi/2\), with at least q zero entries, classify ordered pairs under O(n), or under U(n) in the complex version. Every list satisfying exactly these restrictions is attainable. The dimensions of the ambient space and of both subspaces are also part of the classification when they are not fixed.
reconstruction: The exact dimension-forced zero-angle condition supplies the range requested in the preamble.
fate: The cross-Gram SVD in \citet[Section~3, Theorem~1]{bjorckgolub1973angles} gives the principal angles. Orthogonal principal two-planes plus intersection and unmatched directions give both completeness and the stated dimension restriction.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: Solved classical finite-dimensional problem, including attainability. Replacing the list by its minimum, maximum or average angle discards information.

title: One, two and three subspaces under the general linear group
notes: Problem 6 removes the inner product and asks for complete invariants of one subspace, a pair and an ordered triple, with GL(n) as the acting group.
statement: For one subspace the dimension suffices. For a pair, the dimensions of U,V and \(U\cap V\), together with n, suffice. Over \(\mathbb R\) or \(\mathbb C\), an ordered triple decomposes uniquely into eight one-dimensional membership types indexed by subsets of \(\{1,2,3\}\), and copies of the two-dimensional configuration of three distinct lines \(\operatorname{span}e_1,\operatorname{span}e_2,\operatorname{span}(e_1+e_2)\). The nine multiplicities are complete invariants. All nonnegative multiplicities occur, subject to the ambient dimension \(\sum_Sa_S+2b=n\) and any prescribed subspace dimensions.
reconstruction: The source omits the base field. The stated elementary decomposition is for real or complex vector spaces; its precise multiplicities answer the completeness and range requests.
fate: The introduction of \citet[Section~1]{gelfandponomarev1971quadruples} separates the easy r=2,3 cases from the four-subspace problem. The exact nine-type classification already appears in the prior index at 1972-277.5--6; it is established finite-type linear algebra, not a new 1988 conjecture.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: Solved, with a discrete finite list of building-block types and arbitrary admissible multiplicities. Pairwise intersection dimensions alone do not capture the two-dimensional triple block.

title: Two lines in the Minkowski plane
notes: Problem 7 fixes the quadratic form \(-x_1^2+x_2^2\) and asks for complete invariants of two lines under its preserving group.
statement: For coincident lines the causal type (negative, positive, null) is complete. For two distinct unoriented lines choose nonzero spanning vectors u,v and form \(G=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\langle u,u\rangle&\langle u,v\rangle\\\langle u,v\rangle&\langle v,v\rangle\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). Its equivalence class under \(G\mapsto DGD\), with invertible real diagonal D, is a complete O(1,1) invariant. The attainable matrices are precisely the symmetric two-by-two matrices of signature (1,1), equivalently determinant less than zero. This formulation includes null lines without division by their zero norms.
reconstruction: The diagonal rescaling identifies lines rather than chosen vectors; no orientation or time-orientation constraint is imposed.
fate: This two-dimensional answer follows directly by sending the basis (u,v) to another basis with the same Gram matrix. It is a simple case of the broader form-preserving classification later treated by \citet[Introduction and Theorem~1]{sergeichuk1990pairs}; the elementary case was already available before the talk.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: Solved. An ordinary cosine alone cannot cover spacelike, timelike and null cases.

title: Pairs in finite-dimensional indefinite and degenerate forms
notes: Problem 8 extends the pair problem to higher Minkowski dimensions, arbitrary indefinite signature, and degenerate forms such as \(x_1^2+x_2^2\) on \(\mathbb R^3\).
statement: Fix a finite-dimensional vector space over a field of characteristic different from two with a symmetric, skew-symmetric or Hermitian form F, allowing degeneracy, and two labelled subspaces. Classify triples \((V_F;U_1,U_2)\) up to form-preserving linear isomorphisms carrying each labelled subspace to its counterpart. Sergeichuk gives a complete canonical decomposition for this problem, up to the classification of the Hermitian forms over the relevant fields; for the real symmetric setting these residual forms are determined by their inertia. Isometry blocks, their multiplicities and their allowed field parameters are the complete data, rather than only ordinary principal-angle numbers.
reconstruction: The field, form type, labelled nature and isometry category are fixed explicitly. The notebook asks only the real symmetric cases; the cited theorem treats a broader family.
fate: \citet[Theorem~1]{sergeichuk1990pairs} supplies a precise later classification covering the finite-dimensional indefinite and degenerate formulations. The paper was received on 13 September 1988 and published in 1990; its introduction mentions a partial earlier announcement, so this date is not asserted as the first discovery of every component.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: The finite-dimensional problem has a canonical-form solution. The opened result does not settle the subsequent infinite-dimensional indefinite version, and no such extrapolation is made.

title: Passing from the full orthogonal group to the special group
notes: After the indefinite variants the sheet asks that all listed problems be considered for both O(n) and SO(n).
statement: For a nondegenerate real quadratic space, an O-orbit splits into two SO-orbits exactly when the stabilizer has no determinant-minus-one element; this follows because SO has index two. In the Euclidean ordered-pair case, it splits exactly when all four intersections \(U\cap W,U\cap W^\perp,U^\perp\cap W,U^\perp\cap W^\perp\) vanish. Equivalently, \(n=2k=2m\) and every principal angle lies strictly between zero and \(\pi/2\). Otherwise a reflection in one of those intersections keeps the orbit unsplit. For a degenerate form the full preserving group can have arbitrary nonzero determinant on its radical, so this index-two argument cannot simply be transferred.
reconstruction: The stabilizer criterion and the degeneracy caveat are supplied; the latter prevents an incorrect universal two-orbit claim.
fate: The criterion is an elementary index-two orbit calculation, with the Euclidean stabilizer read from the principal-angle blocks of \citet[Section~3]{bjorckgolub1973angles}. The invariant is augmented by a binary orientation choice exactly in the split case.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: Solved for the stated nondegenerate groups. The notation O(n),SO(n) in the degenerate extension needs a definition and cannot be used to infer an index-two subgroup there.

title: Four subspaces under GL: the Gelfand--Ponomarev classification
notes: Problem 9 asks for complete invariants of a quadruple of subspaces and explicitly calls it the content of the work of Gelfand and Ponomarev.
statement: For an ordered quadruple in a finite-dimensional vector space over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, decomposition into indecomposable quadruples reduces the classification to the discrete families and one-parameter families listed by Gelfand--Ponomarev. With defect \(d=\sum_i\dim U_i-2\dim V\), indecomposable defects are \(-2,-1,0,1,2\); the continuous regular families have defect zero. Their block multiplicities and parameters give complete invariants. Real versions require real canonical blocks rather than silently assuming every eigenvalue is real.
reconstruction: The algebraically closed characteristic-zero hypothesis is the one actually read in the original paper. The labelled order of the four subspaces is retained.
fate: \citet[Section~2, Assertions~1--2; Section~3, Theorem~1]{gelfandponomarev1971quadruples} gives the explicit list and decomposition. It was received on 21 October 1970 and published in 1971. Earlier occurrences are 1970-198.1--13 and 1972-277.7.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: Solved before the talk. The source explicitly attributes existing work; it is not an open classification request in the historical sense.

title: Principal angles of the two tensor subspaces
notes: Problem 10, attributed to A. A. Kirillov junior, gives an inner-product space L, tensors \(a,b\in L\otimes L\), and asks for the angle between \(a\otimes L\) and \(L\otimes b\) in \(L^{\otimes3}\). The preamble explicitly asks which invariant values are attainable.
statement: For a finite-dimensional real or complex Hilbert space of dimension d and nonzero tensors a,b, write their coefficient matrices as A,B in one orthonormal basis. The d principal cosines are the singular values of \((\overline A B)^T/(\|A\|_F\|B\|_F)\). If d is at least two, the complete range is all ordered \(s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_d\ge0\) with \(\sum_js_j\le1\). If d=1 the only cosine is 1. Zero tensors change the subspace dimensions and are excluded from this d-angle statement.
reconstruction: Finite dimension, nonzero tensors and normalization are explicit additions. The real source case is covered; the complex Hilbert variant is also stated. The complete range proof is the chapter annotation, not a result claimed to be in the 1973 paper.
fate: The singular-value interpretation is an application of the established principal-angle theorem of \citet[Section~3, Theorem~1]{bjorckgolub1973angles}. The chapter annotation at Section~\ref{dev:tensor-angles} proves the normalized cross-Gram formula and the exact range directly. It is an explicit solution of this finite-dimensional exercise, with no claim of novelty.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: Solved in the stated finite-dimensional reconstruction, including attainable values. The source only says inner-product space; finite dimension is inferred from its placement before the separate Hilbert-space section, and is recorded rather than hidden.

title: Hilbert pairs, discrete angles and continuous spectral data
notes: Problem 11 asks for a complete invariant of two Hilbert subspaces and for examples with a countable set or a continuum of angle values.
statement: For closed M,N, use the four intersection dimensions and the generic positive contraction C from 1987-735.3. On a separable Hilbert space its spectral measure class together with multiplicity gives the full continuous invariant. For discrete examples take \(C=\operatorname{diag}(\cos\theta_j)\) with \(0<\theta_j<\pi/2\); for a continuum take \(K=L^2(0,1)\), \(Cf(t)=tf(t)\), and \(N=\{(Cf,Sf):f\in K\}\) in \(K\oplus K\). The latter has continuous spectrum [0,1] for C but no eigenvectors at those spectral values.
reconstruction: The projection formulation requires closed subspaces. Separability is imposed only for the familiar measure-and-multiplicity formulation and the displayed examples.
fate: \citet[Theorems~1--3]{halmos1969subspaces} proves the canonical form and completeness. Its 1969 chronology makes this an established answer when the sheet was written.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: Solved for closed Hilbert subspaces. A countable or continuous set of numbers without spectral type and multiplicity is not a complete orbit invariant.

title: The indefinite Hilbert-space version is not specified
notes: Problem 12 asks the same question for a Hilbert space with indefinite metric.
statement: To formulate a definite classification one must specify, for example, a bounded nondegenerate fundamental symmetry J, the topology of the subspaces, whether they are regular for the indefinite form, and the equivalence group of bounded J-unitaries. A degenerate or unbounded form leads to different categories. These choices are absent, and the finite-dimensional canonical-block theorem does not answer all of them.
reconstruction: The possible hypotheses illustrate why the source is insufficient; none is selected and attributed to the author.
fate: \citet{halmos1969subspaces} treats positive Hilbert geometry; \citet[Introduction and Theorem~1]{sergeichuk1990pairs} treats finite-dimensional form spaces. Neither identifies a single exact infinite-dimensional assertion from the unspecified notebook wording.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: No definite remaining open problem can be assigned from this statement alone. This entry is unidentifiable in category, not a declaration that all Krein-space pair classifications are unknown.

title: Realize a prescribed invariant relative to a fixed subspace
notes: The first comment emphasizes the inverse task: given a subspace and an angle invariant, construct another subspace having that invariant.
statement: For a fixed k-plane U in \(\mathbb R^n\), any m-plane principal-angle list satisfying 1987-737.5 is realized by rotating orthogonal principal blocks, using the forced zero-angle intersections to fit the ambient dimension. For a fixed closed Hilbert subspace M, the Halmos data are realizable exactly when the required orthogonal summands fit: \(\dim M=d_{11}+d_{10}+\dim K\) and \(\dim M^\perp=d_{01}+d_{00}+\dim K\). On the generic summands set \(N=\{(Cx,(I-C^2)^{1/2}x):x\in K\}\), and add the chosen intersection summands.
reconstruction: The finite and Hilbert versions are made explicit; no realization claim is made for the undefined indefinite category.
fate: The construction is the inverse of the canonical forms in \citet[Section~3]{bjorckgolub1973angles} and \citet[Theorem~2]{halmos1969subspaces}. Both were established before the seminar.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: Solved for the finite positive and closed Hilbert settings just specified. The cardinal-dimension restrictions are necessary, even when an abstract angle operator has already been chosen.

title: Encode operator similarity by four subspaces
notes: The final comment says that a linear operator can be specified by a quadruple of subspaces.
statement: For \(T:E\to E\), the ordered quadruple \(E\oplus0,\ 0\oplus E,\ \{(x,x)\},\ \{(x,Tx)\}\) in \(E\oplus E\) determines T up to similarity. Any isomorphism preserving the first two subspaces is block diagonal; preservation of the diagonal forces the two blocks to coincide, and preservation of the last graph is exactly the similarity relation. Conversely any similarity gives such a configuration isomorphism.
fate: \citet[Section~1, Example~1]{gelfandponomarev1971quadruples} explicitly gives the graph construction, with the final two labels interchanged. It is already indexed as 1970-198.3.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: Established exact reduction. The source is an expository reminder rather than a new representation theorem.

title: Local polynomial functionals and the variational derivative
notes: The operator is printed as \(L=\partial^N+\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}u_{N-1}\partial^i\); functionals are integrals of polynomials in coefficient jets. Equation (3) defines the variational derivative by first variation.
statement: Fix a differential algebra \(\mathcal A\) of differential polynomials in \(a_0,\ldots,a_{N-1}\), with total derivative \(D\), and write \(L=D^N+\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}a_jD^j\). A formal local functional is a class \(\int P\in\mathcal A/D\mathcal A\). Its Euler derivative is \(\delta F/\delta a_j=\sum_{k\ge0}(-D)^k\,\partial P/\partial a_j^{(k)}\). For smooth periodic coefficients this agrees with integration by parts in \(\delta F=\int\sum_j(\delta F/\delta a_j)\delta a_j\).
reconstruction: The independent coefficients are renamed \(a_j\) to avoid silently mixing the source conventions \(u_j\) and \(u_{N-j}\). Periodicity or the formal quotient removes boundary terms.
fate: This formal calculus is established in \citet[Section~1]{gelfanddikii1978jets} and \citet[Section~2]{gelfanddorfman1979hamiltonian}; both precede the seminar. The repeated coefficient subscript in (1) is incompatible with the later independent variations and Miura formula.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: Standard variational calculus. Local functionals form a vector-space quotient; multiplication of densities does not descend to multiplication of their quotient classes.

title: Disjoint additivity does not imply a smooth local density from continuity alone
notes: Gelfand says that increments supported in two disjoint places add independently, and that this property together with continuity forces a finite-jet integral of the displayed type.
statement: On an open subset \(U\subset C^\infty(M)\), the additivity condition is \(F(\phi+\psi+\chi)=F(\phi+\psi)+F(\psi+\chi)-F(\psi)\) when \(\operatorname{supp}\phi\cap\operatorname{supp}\chi=\varnothing\) and all arguments belong to \(U\). Continuity alone is insufficient: \(F(u)=u(x_0)\) is continuous and additive, but its differential is the Dirac distribution, not integration against a smooth density. A precise characterization additionally assumes Bastiani smoothness, each \(DF_u\) a compactly supported smooth density, and smooth dependence of this density on \(u\) in the test-function topology. The conclusion is a finite-jet integral in a neighborhood of each configuration, with order allowed to depend on that neighborhood.
reconstruction: The function space, topology, smooth density requirement and locally bounded jet order are reconstructed from the later theorem; they are not present in the notebook.
fate: \citet[Theorems~I.2 and VI.3]{brouderetal2018functionals}, first circulated 3 May 2017 and published in 2018, proves this characterization with the stated regularity hypotheses. Its locally finite-order conclusion is weaker than a single global bound on jet order.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: The literal continuity-only claim is false. A precise regular version is proved; no general continuity theorem or global finite-order theorem is inferred from it.
speaker: I. M. Gelfand

title: Length and area as local geometric functionals
notes: Length of a curve and area of a surface are listed as local examples before eigenvalue functionals are called transcendental.
statement: For a smooth immersed curve in a Riemannian manifold, length is \(\int |\dot\gamma(t)|\,dt\). For a smooth immersed surface, area is the integral of the square root of the determinant of the induced metric. These densities depend on first jets and are smooth on the open set of immersions. Disjointly supported perturbations therefore have additive increments, provided the perturbations remain in that open set.
reconstruction: The target metric and nondegeneracy of the immersion are supplied.
fate: These are classical examples of the local variational calculus formalized in \citet[Section~1]{gelfanddikii1978jets}; their smooth, rather than polynomial, jet dependence is the geometric extension explicitly allowed in \citet[Section~2, footnote]{gelfanddorfman1979hamiltonian}.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: Established local examples. Smoothness at a degenerate map is not implied: the immersion hypothesis matters for the square-root densities.
speaker: I. M. Gelfand

title: A hierarchy of transcendence defined by variational differentiation
notes: Type zero means local; type one means that \(\delta F/\delta u\) is local; higher types are recursive. The first eigenvalue is a motivation, and the speaker predicts functionals of all types in characteristic-class theory.
statement: The notes do not specify how a function-valued differential, a distributional one-form or a higher variation is to belong to the same class as a scalar functional. Nor do they specify the operator and boundary conditions defining \(\lambda_1\), the treatment of spectral multiplicities, equivalence modulo constants, or the global configuration space. The recursive words therefore do not determine a single classification problem or a theorem that the hierarchy is strict at every level.
reconstruction: No modern differential-cohomology or spectral-invariant theory is silently substituted for the proposed hierarchy.
fate: The named antecedent is identifiable as \citet[Introduction and Section~1]{gabrielovgelfandlosik1976atiyah}, which studies characteristic-class boundary functionals. That concrete paper does not in the sections read formulate the unrestricted recursive hierarchy asserted here; later local-functional characterizations likewise do not settle an unspecified notion of transcendence.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: The general hierarchy remains unidentifiable as a definite theorem from this source. This F classification concerns the missing definition, not an assertion that the named characteristic-class work was never developed.
speaker: I. M. Gelfand

title: The identified Atiyah--Patodi--Singer functional antecedent
notes: Gelfand recalls work with Gabrielov and an uncertainly written Losik concerning characteristic classes and functionals whose variations have a local character.
statement: The identifiable setting is a compact Riemannian manifold with piecewise smooth boundary and a top-degree characteristic form of the tangent bundle. One seeks face terms such that the characteristic integral plus boundary-face integrals depends on the intrinsic boundary metric and topological data. The referenced paper constructs differential forms on faces and a generalized de Rham cocycle formulation. This is a specific geometric problem, distinct from an unrestricted classification of all scalar functionals by successive variations.
reconstruction: The surname is identified bibliographically as M. V. Losik; the precise geometric setting is supplied by the opened primary paper.
fate: \citet[Introduction and Section~1, Definitions~1.1--1.12]{gabrielovgelfandlosik1976atiyah}, received 22 December 1975 and published in 1976, is the exact author/topic match. Its introduction explicitly separates the proposed boundary-functional structure from what is known in general.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: The historical reference is securely identified and predates the talk. Only the introduction and the foundational definitions were read, so no general boundary decomposition beyond their stated scope is certified.

title: Variational calculus for sums and products of local functionals
notes: Gelfand observes that local functionals are not an algebra, asks for calculus on sums and products, and writes a double integral involving jets at two points. He rejects treating the issue as only a formal adjunction of products.
statement: On a specified smooth field space, the algebra generated by local scalar functionals consists of finite sums of finite products. Its differential obeys \(D(FG)=G\,DF+F\,DG\); higher derivatives obey the iterated Leibniz rule and have kernels on products of the base. Products are generally nonlocal: for \(F(u)=\int u\), the mixed second derivative of \(F^2\) in disjointly supported directions \(h,k\) is \(2(\int h)(\int k)\), which need not vanish. A general smooth double-integral kernel need not be a finite sum of separated kernels, so the displayed two-point expression can describe a broader class.
reconstruction: Finite products, arbitrary two-point kernels, and the unspecified philosophical demand for new geometry are distinguished explicitly.
fate: The elementary product calculus predates the talk. A precise later framework for smooth local and multilocal functionals, including locality criteria on products of manifolds, is given in \citet[Sections~II and VII.B--C]{brouderetal2018functionals}, circulated in 2017 and published in 2018. It supplies a useful rigorous setting without identifying a unique geometric axiom that the notebook demands.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: The stated finite-product differentiation problem is settled; a chosen topology and a distinction between finite products and general multilocal kernels remain essential. The broader request to change geometry is not treated as one unresolved conjecture.
speaker: I. M. Gelfand

title: Hamiltonian formalism without multiplication of local functionals
notes: The proposed way out invokes structures introduced by Gelfand and Dorfman, followed by connections, de Rham cohomology and Yang--Baxter brackets.
statement: One precise construction starts with a Lie algebra \(\mathfrak g\) acting on a module \(M\), with no multiplication assumed on \(M\). Its Chevalley--Eilenberg forms and differential give a Cartan calculus. A Hamiltonian operator \(H\) from suitable one-forms to \(\mathfrak g\), with Lie-closed image and closed induced skew form, defines \(\{f,g\}=(Hdf)g\), satisfying Jacobi. In the variational example, \(M=\mathcal A/D\mathcal A\) and \(\mathfrak g\) consists of evolutionary derivations.
reconstruction: The exact Lie-algebra/module construction is identified; the later programme words are not converted into unsupported claims.
fate: \citet[Section~1, Theorems~1.1 and 1.3; Section~2, Theorem~2.1]{gelfanddorfman1979hamiltonian}, received 16 April 1979, states and proves precisely this module-based construction. The subsequent bare references to connections and Yang--Baxter equations do not specify additional theorems to identify.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: Established framework from 1979, directly relevant to the failure of a density quotient to be an algebra. No nonexistent multiplication on the quotient is needed.
speaker: I. M. Gelfand

title: Formal pseudodifferential symbols and composition
notes: Equations (4)--(8) introduce symbol composition, a Laurent series bounded above in powers of \(\xi\), its differential part and its residue. The series is misleadingly labelled \(C(z)[[\xi]]\) and its summation indices disagree.
statement: Over a characteristic-zero differential coefficient algebra, formal pseudodifferential symbols have the form \(A=\sum_{i\le N}a_i(z)\xi^i\), with arbitrarily negative but finitely many positive powers. Composition is \(A\circ B=\sum_{k\ge0}(\partial_\xi^k A)(\partial_z^k B)/k!\); every resulting coefficient is a finite sum. Put \(A_+=\sum_{i\ge0}a_i\xi^i\) and \(\operatorname{res}A=a_{-1}\). The inverse symbol \(D^{-1}\) is formal and is not a chosen analytic integration operator with boundary conditions.
reconstruction: The coefficient algebra, upper boundedness, matching dummy index and distinction between formal and analytic inverse derivatives are supplied.
fate: This symbolic calculus is already used in \citet[Sections~2--5]{gelfanddikii1976fractional}; the original 1976 article and its composition convention were opened. It is foundational background for both Hamiltonian brackets.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: Established formal algebra. The appropriate Laurent notation is \(\mathcal A((\xi^{-1}))\), with the specified noncommutative composition, rather than the ordinary power-series ring in positive powers of \(\xi\).

title: Residue trace and the pseudodifferential variational gradient
notes: The gradient is \(\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\xi^{-j-1}\circ\delta f/\delta u_j\), followed by \(\delta f=\oint\operatorname{res}(\delta L\circ\nabla f)\).
statement: With \(a_j\) the coefficient of \(D^j\), set \(\operatorname{Tr}A=\int\operatorname{res}A\), modulo total derivatives or on the circle, and \(X_F=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}D^{-j-1}\circ(\delta F/\delta a_j)\). Integration by parts gives \(\operatorname{Tr}[A,B]=0\) and \(\delta F=\operatorname{Tr}(\delta L X_F)\). The trace pairing determines the cotangent representative modulo the annihilator of variations of the monic differential operator.
reconstruction: A single coefficient convention and the formal trace quotient are fixed; the residue trace is not confused with the operator trace on a Hilbert space.
fate: The residue-symbol and variational calculus occurs before the talk in \citet{gelfanddikii1976fractional,gelfanddikii1978jets}. The formula is also a direct coefficient check using cyclicity of the integrated residue; no analytic trace-class assertion is involved.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: Exact in formal or periodic variational calculus. The source gradient uses coefficient order \(u_jD^j\), whereas the later Miura line uses \(u_{N-j}D^j\), so the reindexing must be explicit.

title: The first Gelfand--Dikii bracket
notes: Equations (11) and (13) assert that \(\{F,G\}_1=\operatorname{Tr}([L,X_F]X_G)\) gives a Lie bracket on the stated functionals.
statement: For monic scalar differential operators of fixed positive order over the differential-polynomial algebra, use the residue gradient of item 1987-738.9. The map \(J_{1,L}(X)=[L,X]_+\) is Hamiltonian, and the displayed pairing is a skew bracket satisfying Jacobi on local functionals. The negative part of \([L,X_F]\) does not contribute when paired with the negative-order representative \(X_G\). The leading coefficient is fixed; the coefficient of \(D^{N-1}\) is constant along these Hamiltonian vector fields.
reconstruction: The fixed-order space, quotient by total derivatives and harmless projection under the trace are made explicit.
fate: This is established before the talk. \citet[Section~5, Examples~2--3]{kupershmidtwilson1981modifying} states the exact formula and explains its restriction to zero subleading coefficient; \citet[Sections~10--11]{gelfanddikii1976fractional} supplies an earlier formal variational Lie-bracket construction.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: The Jacobi assertion is proved in the specified formal setting; it is not a new open question in this report. Finite products of actual scalar functionals can be included by the Leibniz rule.

title: The second bracket, compatibility, and the need for reduction
notes: Equation (12) gives \(J_{2,L}(X)=L(XL)_+-(LX)_+L\), and equation (13) asserts the Lie property. The subsequent examples put the subleading coefficient equal to zero.
statement: The pairing \(\{F,G\}_2=\operatorname{Tr}(J_{2,L}(X_F)X_G)\) is Poisson on monic scalar differential operators with all lower coefficients variable. It is compatible with the first bracket: every constant linear combination is Poisson. To pass to \(a_{N-1}=0\), the cotangent representative must be corrected by a \(D^{-N}\) term so that \(\operatorname{res}[X,L]=0\); the resulting Hamiltonian vector field is tangent to the constraint. Merely inserting \(a_{N-1}=0\) in the unreduced formula is insufficient.
reconstruction: Compatibility and the tangency correction are supplied from the proved formulation. The source sign is retained, and its missing reduction is not concealed.
fate: \citet[Section~5, Examples~4--6; Theorems~8.6 and 11.2]{kupershmidtwilson1981modifying} gives the bracket with the opposite overall sign, proves the Hamiltonian property and explains the reduction. Its bibliography identifies the 1978 Gelfand--Dikii IPM preprint136 mentioned in the notebook. \citet[Sections~1 and 6]{khovanova1986gelfand} uses precisely the notebook sign.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: Established before March1988. Overall sign changes preserve the Poisson property, but an omitted reduction changes the actual bracket and the Virasoro normalization.

title: The order-two example is Virasoro, but the printed mode constants disagree
notes: For \(L=D^2+u\), the notes set \(F_n=\frac12(2\pi i)^{-1}\oint u(z)z^{n+1}dz\) and assert \(\{F_n,F_m\}=(n-m)F_{n+m}+(n^3-n)\delta_{n+m,0}/12\).
statement: Fix \(\operatorname{Tr}=(2\pi i)^{-1}\oint\operatorname{res}\) and exactly the notebook pairing \(\{F,G\}=\operatorname{Tr}((J_2X_F)X_G)\). After reduction, the coefficient operator is \(J_u(f)=-\frac12D^3f-2uDf-(Du)f\). For the displayed \(F_n\), integration by parts gives \[\{F_n,F_m\}=\frac{m-n}{2}F_{n+m}-\frac{n^3-n}{8}\delta_{n+m,0}.\] Reversing the pairing reverses both signs. Suitable rescalings recover a Virasoro bracket, but they cannot be omitted while retaining the stated modes and claiming the printed constants.
reconstruction: The normalized residue, reduction and order of the pairing are all stated so that the correction is reproducible. The ordinary Fourier/Laurent identity is used, not a quantum normal-ordering correction.
fate: \citet[Section~7, Lemma~6 and its preceding formulas]{khovanova1986gelfand} explicitly gives the reduced order-two operator and its coadjoint Virasoro interpretation, published in1986. The mode calculation above follows directly from that operator and was independently checked during this task.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: The structural Virasoro identification is established. Under the explicit fixed convention the source mode formula is false; its numerical constants are not certified by an appeal to the structural identification alone.

title: The order-three bracket and the primary spin-three field
notes: For \(L=D^3+u_2D+u_3\), the notes give a Virasoro bracket for \(u_2\), a mixed coefficient \(2n-m\), and an incomplete \(u_3,u_3\) formula containing a convolution quadratic in \(u_2\).
statement: The reduced order-three second Gelfand--Dikii bracket is the classical \(W_3\) Poisson algebra. For the raw operator coefficients, the spin-three primary is \(w_3=u_3-\frac12Du_2\). Indeed, infinitesimal coordinate covariance gives \(\delta_f u_2=fDu_2+2(Df)u_2+2D^3f\) and \(\delta_f u_3=fDu_3+3(Df)u_3+u_2D^2f+D^4f\), so \(\delta_f w_3=fDw_3+3(Df)w_3\). The pure spin-three mixed mode formula belongs to this corrected field. The self-bracket has quadratic stress-tensor terms, but the notebook ellipsis is not a complete set of defining relations.
reconstruction: The reduction and primary field change are supplied explicitly. No exact coefficient for the unfinished quadratic convolution is invented.
fate: The Virasoro inclusion is treated in \citet[Section~9]{khovanova1986gelfand}. \citet[Sections~1 and 3]{lukyanov1988quantization} relates these classical brackets to their quantum \(W\)-algebra construction. The displayed primary change follows directly from the two coordinate-variation equations and clarifies the raw-coefficient ambiguity.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: The classical algebra was known before the talk. Its identification does not validate the omitted terms or the numerical central coefficients of the notebook. A pure primary mixed bracket for the unchanged raw \(u_3\) is incorrect.

title: The classical Miura map is Poisson
notes: The product \(L=(D+v_1)\cdots(D+v_N)\) defines the coefficient fields, and the modes of the \(v_i\) have independent Heisenberg brackets \(h\,n\delta_{ij}\delta_{n+m,0}\).
statement: Take the \(v_i\) as independent differential variables with the constant diagonal first-order Hamiltonian structure. Expanding the ordered product makes every coefficient of \(L\) a differential polynomial in them. The induced bracket on those coefficients is the second Gelfand--Dikii bracket, with the common overall scale and sign fixed by the chosen pairing. Reduction to zero subleading coefficient requires the corresponding constraint \(\sum_i v_i=0\) and the reduced current bracket; independent currents cannot simply retain their unreduced brackets after that constraint.
reconstruction: Formal differential variables, factor order, normalization and the separate constrained-current reduction are specified.
fate: \citet[Theorem~11.5, p.~436; Theorem~8.6 for the reduced case]{kupershmidtwilson1981modifying} proves the constant-current realization. The original cover gives1981, whereas current Springer metadata gives1980; receipt was February1980 and revision18August1980. \citet[equation~(1.5)]{lukyanov1988quantization} recalls the classical theorem before quantizing it.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: Established Poisson realization. It is a nonlinear differential-polynomial map, not a globally invertible change of coefficient functions on every analytic function space.

title: Known first-order factors give a solution by quadratures
notes: Gelfand observes that \((D+v_1)(D+v_2)y=f\) can be solved by quadratures and compares differential Galois theory with solving algebraic equations by radicals.
statement: If continuous \(v_1,v_2,f\) are known on an interval, put \(w=(D+v_2)y\) and \(V_i(x)=\int_{x_0}^xv_i(t)\,dt\). Then \(w=e^{-V_1}(C_1+\int_{x_0}^x e^{V_1(t)}f(t)\,dt)\) and \(y=e^{-V_2}(C_2+\int_{x_0}^xe^{V_2(t)}w(t)\,dt)\). These formulas solve the factored equation with two initial constants. The assertion presupposes known factors; it does not supply them over a prescribed differential field or impose global periodic boundary conditions.
reconstruction: The two elementary integrating-factor formulas give the precise content of the remark without attributing a general differential-Galois theorem to it.
fate: This is the classical integrating-factor calculation. The factorization and differential-field viewpoint are also explicit in \citet[Section~9]{kupershmidtwilson1981modifying}. The brief mention of Picard--Vessiot theory is an analogy, not a complete solvability criterion stated in the source.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: Correct under the stated coefficient and factorization assumptions. Factoring a general differential operator can be the difficult step, and quadratures need not lie in the original coefficient field.
speaker: I. M. Gelfand

title: Nonlinear Poisson relations do not destroy the Lie property
notes: The notes say that a Lie algebra has become isomorphic to a quadratic algebra that is not a Lie algebra; Khovanova is named, and an unspecific comparison with Dynkin follows.
statement: A Poisson algebra is always a Lie algebra under its bracket, even when brackets of selected generators are quadratic polynomials rather than linear combinations of those generators. Thus the span of the chosen coefficient fields may fail to be Lie-closed, while the full Poisson algebra still satisfies Jacobi. The Miura map is a Poisson realization, and the existence of a nonlinear formula does not make it an isomorphism onto the entire current algebra.
reconstruction: The meanings of generator span, Poisson algebra and realization are separated; no specific Dynkin theorem is guessed.
fate: \citet[Section~1, Lemma~1; Section~7]{khovanova1986gelfand} explicitly constructs Gelfand--Dikii Lie algebras, directly contradicting the literal denial of a Lie structure. \citet[Theorem~11.5]{kupershmidtwilson1981modifying} states the Miura restriction theorem, not a universal isomorphism. The Dynkin remark names no definite algebra or theorem.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: The literal formulation is false. The meaningful distinction is between a linearly closed generating space and nonlinear Poisson relations in the larger algebra.

title: Quantum Miura coefficients from Heisenberg currents
notes: The factors are normal ordered, \(L(z)=:(D+v_1(z))\cdots(D+v_N(z)):\), and the question is which relations the coefficient fields satisfy.
statement: Work with formal radially ordered Heisenberg currents whose singular products are \(v_i(z)v_j(w)\sim h\delta_{ij}(z-w)^{-2}\). Choose the usual mode normal ordering and expand \(L=D^N+\sum_{j=1}^N W_jD^{N-j}\). This defines coefficient fields as normally ordered differential polynomials. The problem is to compute their singular operator products and prove closure, rather than to multiply arbitrary unregularized operator-valued distributions at a point.
reconstruction: The formal mode algebra, radial order and normal-ordering convention supply the operator meaning suppressed by the notation.
fate: \citet[Section~1, equations~(1.1)--(1.5)]{lukyanov1988quantization} makes precisely this construction. The paper was received25February1988, before the21March report, and published later in1988; it acknowledges Radul. The theorem belongs to Lukyanov, whom Radul explicitly reports.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: The construction is established. The subsequent items identify the regularity equation and closure theorem answering the stated relation problem.

title: Quadratic closure and explicit hypergeometric coefficients
notes: Equation (24) gives a sum of singular powers with coefficient products, but the bracket signs are ambiguous; the constants are said to involve hypergeometric functions.
statement: The quantum Miura coefficient fields satisfy quadratic singular-product relations of the form \[W_i(z)W_j(w)+\sum_{k=2}^{i+j}\frac{\sum_{p+q=i+j-k}C_{ij}^{pq}(k)\,W_p(z)W_q(w)}{(z-w)^k}=O(1),\] with \(W_0=1\) and numerical coefficients depending on the quantum parameter. Their explicit formulas are obtained from the auxiliary coefficients expressed through generalized hypergeometric functions. This is a statement about ordered operator products and their singular parts; blindly interpreting every square bracket in the notebook as a commutator does not give the published theorem.
reconstruction: The ordered-product interpretation and finite singular sum are supplied from the publication; the unverified handwritten sign choices are not silently certified.
fate: \citet[Theorem~1, equation~(1.6), and equations~(2.18)--(2.21)]{lukyanov1988quantization} proves this closure and gives the coefficient prescription. Theorem 2 gives the associated reduced \(W_N\) construction after the current constraint is imposed with its appropriate covariance.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: The definite relation problem is solved in the identified1988 work. The source formula records the correct quadratic structure, but its ambiguous bracket notation is not a fully reliable literal presentation.

title: A schematic quantum inverse-scattering exchange analogy
notes: The final sentence compares the regularity formula with the quantum inverse-scattering method and writes \(L(z)L(w)=R^{-1}L(w)L(z)R\), without defining \(R\).
statement: No auxiliary space, operator \(R\), spectral-parameter dependence, tensor-leg convention or equality modulo regular terms is specified. The written identity therefore does not determine a separate Yang--Baxter or exchange theorem. In particular it cannot replace the already identified conjugated regularity relation by an exact unrestricted operator equality.
fate: \citet[Section~2.1, after equation~(2.6)]{lukyanov1988quantization} explicitly remarks on an analogy with a classical r-matrix, while its proved statement is the regularity relation identified above. No precise additional R-matrix theorem matching the final bare formula was established by the source check.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: Unidentifiable as a distinct exact theorem; retained as an analogy. The surrounding quantum closure result is known and is not assigned open status because this final shorthand lacks a definition.

title: Representations of an acyclic quiver
notes: A quiver is called a directed graph without cycles; \(M(\Lambda,\Omega)\) is its representation category.
statement: For a finite quiver \(Q=(Q_0,Q_1)\) with no oriented cycles over a field \(k\), let \(\operatorname{rep}_kQ\) consist of finite-dimensional vertex spaces and linear arrow maps. It is an abelian hereditary category, equivalent to finite-dimensional modules over \(kQ\).
reconstruction: Finiteness, the coefficient field, and oriented rather than undirected cycles are made explicit.
fate: This is the framework of \citet[\S1]{bernsteingelfandponomarev1973coxeter}; the derived-category report uses it in \citet[\S1]{parthasarathy1988tstructures}.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: established under the stated hypotheses.

title: Orientation independence and its graph hypothesis
notes: The lemma says \(\mathcal D(\Lambda,\Omega_1)\simeq\mathcal D(\Lambda,\Omega_2)\) for different orientations, with reflections as proof.
statement: A reflection at a source or sink induces an equivalence of bounded derived categories. Hence orientations joined by such reflections have equivalent categories; in particular this holds for any two orientations of a finite tree, including every Dynkin tree.
reconstruction: The tree or reflection-equivalence hypothesis is essential; the drawing alone does not establish it.
fate: \citet[Propositions~1.4 and~1.6]{parthasarathy1988tstructures} constructs the derived reflection equivalences from BGP functors. An unrestricted assertion for all acyclic orientations of an arbitrary graph is not supplied by this argument. Derived equivalence under tilting was already proved in \citet[\S1.7, Corollary, p.~344]{happel1987derived}, published in 1987 after an Ottawa 1984 announcement; applied to a source/sink reflection, it supplies the pre-talk derived-category formulation.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: derived reflection invariance is established; the notebook' s unrestricted orientation wording should not be used as a theorem.

title: Hearts with the same derived category
notes: Find abelian subcategories \(\mathcal A\subset\mathcal D\) with \(\mathcal D^\ell(\mathcal A)=\mathcal D\); the notes say all are found and characterized by Dynkin graphs.
statement: Let k be an algebraically closed field and Q a finite acyclic quiver. Describe bounded t-structures on \(D^b(\operatorname{rep}_kQ)\) whose heart \(\mathcal A\) is a finite-length abelian k-category with a projective generator and finite-dimensional Hom spaces, and whose realization functor \(D^b(\mathcal A)\to D^b(\operatorname{rep}_kQ)\) is an equivalence.
reconstruction: The superscript is read as bounded derived category, and abelian subcategory is interpreted as a heart. The stated finiteness conditions prevent a claim about arbitrary embedded abelian categories.
fate: \citet[Theorems~3.3, 7.1 and~8.5]{parthasarathy1988tstructures} gives a criterion for the specified t-structure data, relates the constructed hearts to iterated tilted algebras, and proves completeness in the Dynkin case. It was received 15 February 1988, revised 13 May, and published in December 1988 by Parthasarathy, whose work Kapranov reports here; receipt alone does not establish public pre-talk circulation of the criterion. The Dynkin algebra classification itself was already \citet[Theorem~5.12, p.~358]{happel1987derived}, published in 1987 after an Ottawa 1984 announcement. Thus the later publication match is the explicit heart-realization approach, not a claim that the Dynkin classification first appeared in 1988. The notebook blanket sentence is broader than either precise formulation.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: the identified finite-type/iterated-tilting classification is established; an unrestricted classification is not asserted.

title: A source reflection retains a two-term complex
notes: At a source \(\alpha\), replace \(V_\alpha\) by the cokernel of \(V_\alpha\to\bigoplus_{\alpha\to\beta}V_\beta\); vectors killed by every arrow are lost, so retain the map as a complex.
statement: The ordinary reflection uses that cokernel and reverses the incident arrows. Its total derived functor uses the two-term complex, with a degree convention fixed once, and preserves the kernel information. This gives the source reflection equivalence.
reconstruction: The vertex is required to be a source and the cone shift is conventional.
fate: BGP's source/sink functors appear in \citet[\S1]{bernsteingelfandponomarev1973coxeter}; the derived construction is explicit in \citet[\S1, Proposition~1.6]{parthasarathy1988tstructures}. Derived equivalence under tilting was already proved in \citet[\S1.7, Corollary, p.~344]{happel1987derived}, published in 1987 after an Ottawa 1984 announcement; applied to a source/sink reflection, it supplies the pre-talk derived-category formulation.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: established under the stated hypotheses.

title: Derived categories as a language for projective bundles
notes: Gelfand says classification of vector bundles on \(\mathbb{CP}^n\) can only be done in the language of derived categories.
statement:
An established precise tool is the exceptional collection
\[
 (\mathcal O,\mathcal O(1),\ldots,\mathcal O(n))
\]
on \(\mathbb P^n\) and the resulting resolution of coherent sheaves by explicit complexes. This does not prove the literal exclusivity of a mathematical language or classify all bundles.
reconstruction: The resolution is an illustrative reconstruction of the method, not an assertion that Gelfand stated a classification theorem.
fate: \citet{beilinson1978coherent} supplies the relevant pre-1988 construction. The word only is methodological emphasis rather than a theorem.

title: Linear independence as a matroid
notes: Gelfand gives linearly independent systems of vectors as the example of a matroid.
statement: For a finite indexed family \((v_e)_{e\in E}\) in a vector space, let \(\mathcal I=\{I\subset E:(v_e)_{e\in I}\text{ is linearly independent}\}\). Heredity and the exchange axiom make \((E,\mathcal I)\) a matroid.
fate: This is the elementary representable-matroid example in \citet[opening definitions]{oxleybriefly}. Compare the matroid/lattice occurrence 1985-658.12; no new problem is posed here.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: established under the stated hypotheses.
speaker: I. M. Gelfand

title: Rado transversals and the induced rank formula
notes: For a relation \(\varphi\subset M_1\times M_2\), the asserted rank is \(r_2(A)=\min_{B\subset A}(r_1(\varphi(B))+|A-B|)\).
statement: Let \(M_1\) be a finite matroid and \(M_2\) finite. A subset \(I\subset M_2\) is independent when it admits distinct representatives in \(M_1\), related to its elements by \(\varphi\), that form an independent set of the first matroid. These sets form a matroid, and the displayed minimum is its rank on \(A\).
reconstruction: Finite ground sets and the independent-transversal definition are supplied explicitly.
fate: The independence-transversal theorem is \citet{rado1942independence}; Hall's special case predates it. The publisher-deposited Crossref metadata for Rado were opened and checked; the full original theorem was not successfully opened in this run.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: established under the stated hypotheses.

title: Hall's marriage theorem and the free-matroid reduction
notes: The union condition for sets \(B(n)\subset M\) yields an injection \(f:N\to M\); the notes write \(f(n)\subset B(n)\) and declare all subsets of \(N\) independent.
statement: For finite \(N\), an injection satisfying \(f(n)\in B(n)\) exists iff \(|\bigcup_{n\in K}B(n)|\geq|K|\) for every \(K\subset N\). To derive this from Rado with representatives in \(M\), use the free matroid on \(M\), whose rank is cardinality.
reconstruction: Membership replaces subset inclusion, and the free matroid belongs on the representative ground set \(M\).
fate: \citet[Theorem~1, pp.~27--29]{hall1935representatives} proves precisely this condition; the paper was received and read in April 1934 and published in 1935.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: established under the stated hypotheses.

title: An algorithmic proof of the marriage theorem
notes: There is a proof containing an algorithm.
statement: For a finite bipartite graph, start with a matching and repeatedly augment along alternating paths. If no augmenting path exists while a left vertex is unmatched, its alternating reachable sets violate Hall's condition. Thus the procedure finds a complete left matching under that condition.
reconstruction: The notes do not name a running time or a particular implementation; no algorithmic novelty is inferred.
fate: \citet[proof of Theorem~1]{hall1935representatives} gives a constructive replacement argument. The augmenting-path formulation is an explicit modern reconstruction of the terse algorithmic remark.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: established under the stated hypotheses.

title: A common system of left and right coset representatives
notes: A finite subgroup has representatives that work simultaneously for its left and right cosets; the statement is attributed to Birkhoff.
statement: If \(H\leq G\) and \(G\) is finite, there is a set meeting each left coset and each right coset of \(H\) once. More generally finite \(H\) admits such a transversal in arbitrary \(G\), by applying the finite equal-block matching argument within each double coset and choosing these transversals.
reconstruction: For infinite \(G\), each double coset has equally many left and right cosets because \(H\) is finite; a choice of the finite matchings is used.

title: The parallel postulate and non-Euclidean models

reconstruction: The formal independence statement is relative to an axiom system and consistency assumption, neither specified in the remark.

title: Classical construction impossibilities
notes: Angle trisection and circle quadrature are linked with the development of Galois theory.
statement: With an unmarked straightedge and compass, an arbitrary given angle cannot be trisected, and a square of the same area as a given circle cannot be constructed. The first follows from a cubic obstruction, for example trisection of \(60^\circ\); the second follows from the transcendence of \(\pi\).
reconstruction: The allowed instruments and the general rather than every-angle quantifier are supplied.

present_status: As of 11 November 2026: established under the stated hypotheses.

title: Fermat's equation and the later modularity proof
notes: Fermat's problem is linked to Kummer's ideals and algebraic geometry; Faltings appears in a marginal annotation.
statement: For every integer \(n>2\), there are no positive integers \(a,b,c\) with \(a^n+b^n=c^n\). Finiteness of rational points on a fixed genus-greater-than-one curve does not by itself prove this nonexistence statement.

title: Four colours and computer-assisted proof
notes: The four-colour problem is connected with computer mathematics.
statement: Every finite loopless planar graph admits a proper vertex colouring with at most four colours. The 1976 Appel--Haken proof combined unavoidable configurations with certified reducibility computations.

title: Exceptional bundles and ordered exceptional collections
notes: For bundles \(E_1,E_2,E_3\) on \(\mathbb P^2\), the notes impose scalar endomorphisms, vanishing positive self-Ext, and backward Ext vanishing.

An ordered exceptional collection satisfies \(\operatorname{Ext}^p(E_j,E_i)=0\) for every \(p\) and \(j>i\). Here the objects are algebraic vector bundles on \(\mathbb P^2\).

title: Exceptional ranks satisfy the Markov equation
notes: The ranks \(x_1,x_2,x_3\) of the exceptional triple satisfy \(x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2=3x_1x_2x_3\).

reconstruction: Fullness and positive ranks are stated explicitly; this is not a rank equation for arbitrary triples of exceptional bundles.
fate: \citet[Theorem~3.2]{rudakov1988markov} gives the rank identity. The Russian original appeared in 1988, volume 52, issue 1; the English translation in 1989. Its submission was in April 1986.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: established under the stated hypotheses.

title: Realization of positive Markov triples by bundles
notes: Conversely, the notes say every integer solution is obtained.
statement: Every positive integer Markov triple is realized by the ranks of an exceptional triple of bundles on \(\mathbb P^2\), obtained from the standard triple by the appropriate mutations and ordering conventions. Zero or negative integral solutions are not positive bundle ranks.
reconstruction: The word integer is restricted to positive integer, as required by ranks.
fate: \citet[Introduction and Theorem~4.2]{rudakov1988markov} constructs the Markov tree of adjacent exceptional bundles. This does not assert the separate Markov uniqueness conjecture that a largest entry determines the triple.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: established under the stated hypotheses.

title: Mutation and the braid action on the plane
notes: The braid group acts on exceptional triples, transitively in the plane case.
statement: Left and right mutations of adjacent exceptional objects obey the braid relation and act on full exceptional collections. On the smooth quadric surface, the four line bundles
\[
 \mathcal O,\quad\mathcal O(1,0),\quad\mathcal O(0,1),\quad\mathcal O(1,1)

generate a standard helix. Mutations construct other helices; every helix and every exceptional bundle is constructible in Rudakov's precise sense.

title: Finite, tame, and wild representation problems
notes: Gelfand distinguishes no parameters, one parameter, and at least two parameters, comparing the last with classifying pairs of matrices.
statement: For a fixed finite-dimensional algebra over an algebraically closed field, finite representation type means finitely many indecomposable isomorphism classes; tame type permits finitely many one-parameter families in each dimension, with finitely many exceptions; wildness means that the problem of modules over the free algebra in two generators embeds in the representation problem. title: An open orbit is not automatic in a wild problem
notes: Gelfand says an unsolvable classification always contains a solvable part, adding an open orbit.

In simultaneous conjugation of pairs of \(n\times n\) complex matrices, the invariant \(\operatorname{tr}(A)\) varies, so no orbit can be dense in the full affine space of pairs. This already refutes an unconditional open-orbit assertion.

title: Self-Ext vanishing and infinitesimal rigidity

title: Exceptional pairs require exceptional individual objects

The resulting exceptional pair is \((R,E)\), not \((F,R)\). In general use the distinguished triangle \(L_EF\to\operatorname{RHom}(E,F)\otimes E\to F\to L_EF[1]\).

notes: Mutation gives the braid-group action; Gelfand recalls BGP and recommends studying quiver representations and derived categories for spectral theory.

title: Constructible sheaves and complexes
notes: A sheaf is locally constant of finite rank on each stratum; for a complex the condition is on its cohomology sheaves, not on its terms.
statement: For a complex algebraic variety with a finite algebraic Whitney stratification \(\mathcal S\), \(D^b_{\mathcal S}(X;k)\) consists of bounded sheaf complexes whose cohomology restricts to finite-rank local systems on every stratum. Analytic versions use locally finite stratifications.
reconstruction: Boundedness, coefficients, Whitney regularity and finiteness conventions are supplied.
fate: \citet[Chapter~8]{kashiwaraschapira1985microlocal} treats the constructibility conditions. The notebook correctly distinguishes cohomological constructibility from a particular complex of representatives.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: established under the stated hypotheses.

title: Singular support requires uniform local tests
notes: A nonzero covector is excluded from \(SS(\mathcal F)\) when a relative cohomology group for a function with that differential vanishes; the notes say the choice of function does not matter.
statement: For a bounded constructible complex on a real manifold, \((x,\xi)\notin SS(F)\) means there is an open conic neighbourhood on which all local cohomology tests \((R\Gamma_{\{\phi\geq\phi(y)\}}F)_y\) vanish whenever \((y,d\phi_y)\) lies in that neighbourhood. Holomorphic Morse tests describe the corresponding complex-constructible microsupport, with their normalizations.
reconstruction: The precise real-test definition is supplied to avoid interpreting a schematic single-function test as an invariant definition.
fate: The uniform-neighbourhood condition is in \citet[Definition~0.1 and \S3.1]{kashiwaraschapira1985microlocal}. Vanishing for a single arbitrary chosen function is not the complete definition.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: established under the stated hypotheses.

title: The zero-section part of singular support
notes: If the complex is nonzero, the entire zero section is added; an acyclic complex has empty singular support.
statement: One has \(SS(F)\cap T_X^*X=\operatorname{supp}(F)\), where the right side is embedded as zero covectors. Thus \(SS(0)=\varnothing\), but a nonzero skyscraper sheaf does not contain zero covectors over other points.
reconstruction: \ours{}
fate: \citet[\S3.1, basic properties of microsupport]{kashiwaraschapira1985microlocal} gives the support relation. The skyscraper example on P001452 itself detects the error.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: the support-restricted statement is standard; the unconditional addition of the zero section is false.

title: Complex constructibility gives a conic Lagrangian support
notes: \(SS(F)\) is an analytic conic Lagrangian set with finitely many irreducible components; ideal involutivity is presented as equivalent.
statement: For complex-constructible \(F\), its microsupport, identified with the complex cotangent bundle, is a closed complex-conic Lagrangian analytic subset. Components are locally finite; global finiteness follows in the finite algebraic setting. Involutivity of the ideal gives coisotropicity, and is equivalent to the Lagrangian condition only with the half-dimensional hypothesis.
reconstruction: Complex constructibility and the dimension/finiteness qualifications are made explicit.
fate: \citet[Theorem~6.4.1 and Chapter~8]{kashiwaraschapira1985microlocal} supplies involutivity and the constructible Lagrangian characterization.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: established under the stated hypotheses.

title: Irreducible conic Lagrangians are conormal closures
notes: An irreducible conic Lagrangian \(Y\subset T^*X\) is \(N^*Z\) for \(Z=\pi(Y)\), with closure over the smooth locus understood.
statement: In the algebraic setting, a closed irreducible conic Lagrangian subset is the closure of \(T^*_{Z_{\mathrm{sm}}}X\) for the irreducible subvariety \(Z=\overline{\pi(Y)}\). The analytic assertion is local. This follows by annihilating tangent vectors to a generic smooth image under the canonical symplectic form and comparing dimensions.
reconstruction: Closedness, algebraic/local analytic context and closure of the image are specified.
fate: This is the conormal geometry underlying \citet[Chapter~8]{kashiwaraschapira1985microlocal}. The argument and the closure conventions are elementary reconstruction of the lemma as stated.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: established under the stated hypotheses.

title: Morse transversality to a singular support
notes: The graph of \(df\) must meet \(Y\) only at smooth points and transversely; examples are the zero section and a smooth conormal.
statement: For a holomorphic function \(f\) and conic Lagrangian \(Y\), a microlocal Morse point is a transverse intersection of \(\Gamma_{df}\) with \(Y_{\mathrm{sm}}\), away from the singular part of \(Y\). For \(Y=T_X^*X\) this is an ordinary nondegenerate critical point; for \(Y=T_Z^*X\) with smooth \(Z\), it is a nondegenerate critical point of \(f|_Z\).
reconstruction: The criterion is local at an isolated transverse intersection, not a demand that a global function exist with every required property.
fate: This is the test-function construction used in \citet[Introduction and \S1]{gelfandmacphersonvilonen2005microlocal}, building on the earlier microlocal theory. The crossed-out extra demand \(df\ne0\) is not part of the general conormal criterion.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: established under the stated hypotheses.

title: Perversity detected by Morse groups
notes: All Morse relative hypercohomology groups must occur in degree zero; a parenthetical remark instead says first degree.
statement: With the convention that \(k_X[\dim_{\mathbb C}X]\) is perverse, a constructible bounded complex is perverse exactly when its normalized local Morse groups are concentrated in degree zero. For an isolated Morse test, these can be represented by \(\mathbb H^j(B,B\cap f^{-1}(\varepsilon);F)\), after fixing the vanishing-cycle shift convention.
reconstruction: The normalized Morse functor rather than an unlabelled cone fixes the degree convention.
fate: \citet[Theorem~9.5.2 and Introduction]{kashiwaraschapira1985microlocal} gives the microlocal characterization. The degree-one parenthesis can reflect the unshifted vanishing-cycle cone, and cannot coexist literally with degree zero without specifying the shift.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: established under the stated hypotheses.

title: Basic perverse sheaves and the closed-embedding hypothesis
notes: Examples are a skyscraper, \(\mathbb C_X[n]\), and \(\mathbb C_Z[\dim Z]\) extended by zero from a smooth subset, or an intersection-cohomology complex.
statement: A finite-dimensional skyscraper is perverse. On a smooth complex \(n\)-fold a local system shifted by \(n\) is perverse. For a closed smooth embedding \(i:Z\hookrightarrow X\), \(i_*L[\dim Z]\) is perverse. For an arbitrary open or locally closed embedding, ordinary extension by zero need not be perverse; intermediate extension is the appropriate canonical construction.
reconstruction: Closedness is restored to the zero-extension example; the singular case uses intersection cohomology rather than a constant sheaf.
fate: \citet[Theorem~9.5.2]{kashiwaraschapira1985microlocal} gives the perverse framework, and \citet{goreskymacpherson1983intersection} is the intersection-cohomology source.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: established under the stated hypotheses.

title: Singular support does not canonically recover every stratum
notes: An explicitly approximate remark identifies strata with projections of irreducible components of \(SS(F)\).
statement: The projections recover certain closed singular-support loci, not a unique stratification. A compatible Whitney stratification may be refined without changing \(F\) or \(SS(F)\); even the constant sheaf admits many such refinements.
reconstruction: \ours{} The notebook already flags the assertion as approximate; its strongest literal interpretation is rejected.
fate: \citet[Chapter~8]{kashiwaraschapira1985microlocal} relates constructibility to unions of conormals, which is weaker than a unique reconstruction of the chosen strata.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: only the conormal-support relation is valid; no canonical full stratification follows.

title: Morse groups form a microlocal local system with a twist
notes: At a smooth covector \(z\), define \(\Phi(F)_z=H^0(U,f^{-1}(\varepsilon);F)\) for \(df=z\), claiming no dependence on \(f\).
statement: On the smooth locus of a fixed singular support, normalized Morse data vary locally constantly after accounting for the Maslov/orientation data of the test-function Hessian. The natural object is a twisted local system (or a local system on the appropriate bundle of Morse data), not canonically an untwisted local system from the covector alone.

title: Configurations, reducibility, and unavoidability
notes: A configuration is a triangulated disc; an unavoidable collection occurs in every triangulation, and a reducible member cannot occur in a smallest counterexample.
statement: In a finite simple plane triangulation, a configuration specifies a finite near-triangulation together with the required degrees of its internal vertices and a boundary ring. Reducibility means that an occurrence can be replaced by a smaller graph whose four-colouring can be lifted, possibly using Kempe changes. An unavoidable set is one occurring in every triangulation of the relevant reduced class.
reconstruction: Degree and boundary data and the relevant class of minimal counterexamples are restored.
fate: \citet[\S3]{gonthier2005fourcolour} states the established proof structure, already present in the 1977 Appel--Haken proof. An arbitrary disc triangulation without embedding and degree data is not the complete configuration specification.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: established under the stated hypotheses.

title: An unavoidable reducible family proves four-colourability
notes: The main idea is to combine the two definitions and induct on the number of vertices.
statement: If every minimal non-four-colourable plane triangulation contains a member of a fixed family, and every member is reducible, no minimal counterexample exists. After deleting duplicate edges, a finite loopless planar graph with at least three vertices extends to a simple plane triangulation; smaller graphs are immediate. Restricting a four-colouring yields the theorem.
fate: The proof scheme was realized in \citet{appelhakenkoch1977reducibility}; \citet[\S3, parts I--II]{gonthier2005fourcolour} states its formalized version.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: established under the stated hypotheses.

title: The cosine addition identity as a spherical-function example
notes: Gelfand says his spherical-function theory arose from \(\cos(\alpha+\beta)+\cos(\alpha-\beta)=2\cos\alpha\cos\beta\), using translations and reflections of the line.

title: Degree-four vertices are reducible by a Kempe argument
notes: For four neighbours with all four colours, either the 1--3 Kempe path is absent, or its planar separation prevents a 2--4 path; a colour swap frees a colour.
statement: In a plane triangulation, a vertex of degree four cannot belong to a minimal non-four-colourable graph. Remove it and colour the smaller graph. If the four cyclic neighbours use four different colours, disjoint alternating 1--3 and 2--4 connecting paths cannot both exist in the punctured plane; swap on a component of one colour pair and extend the colouring.

title: Boundary colourings and Kempe closure
notes: Some boundary colourings extend into a configuration, others do not; a computer searches for recolourings as in the previous example.
statement: For a fixed finite ring configuration, enumerate proper four-colourings of the ring and the subset extendible through the interior. Reducibility tests combine this finite data with the permitted noncrossing Kempe-chain pairing information from the exterior. Arbitrary swaps of boundary colours without such compatibility do not establish reducibility.

title: The drawn configuration is the Birkhoff diamond
notes: The scan draws a hexagonal ring around four interior vertices and calls it reducible, adding that Fuchs could not prove it.

reconstruction: Identification uses the graph incidence and degree-five internal vertices visible in the scan; no missing proof is attributed to Fuchs.

title: A parallel program for a fixed reducibility test

title: Euler curvature and a first unavoidable set
notes: Using \(V-E+F=2\), \(2E=\sum i\nu_i\), \(3F=2E\), the notes derive \(\sum(6-i)\nu_i=12\), so a degree-three, four or five vertex exists.
